Hon. IAN MACKENZIE (Vancouver
Centre): Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct the attention of the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) to a question which I asked the other day of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes). This question which appears on page 2807 of Hansard is as follows:
I should like to ask the hon. Minister of Finance what is the policy in general of the federal government in regard to permitting any of the provincial governments to enter the British financial market for refunding purposes.
The reply of the Minister of Finance in part was as follows:
I shall be happy to direct the attention of my right hon. leader who is Minister of External Affairs to the question for any further answer which may be given on Monday.
I direct the attention of the Prime Minister to this matter.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The question raised by the hon. gentleman is obviously one over which this government has no control. So far as I could ascertain at the time we made the last loan in London the tendency was not to permit provincial governments to make issues on the London market. The hon. gentleman knows quite well that that is not an open market and no issues can be made there unless the treasury has given its consent. The treasury at once accorded the Dominion of Canada

consent to make the loan of last fall. While I have no definite information, my conclusion, from what was said and has since been communicated to me by representatives of the provinces, is that it would be very difficult to secure consent for any provincial government to place a loan upon the British market. That is my information at the moment. The hon. gentleman understands, of course, that there is no finality about matters of this kind; they are subject to change, having regard to the conditions that exist at the time that application may be made. And of course-I want to make this perfectly clear-as my colleague suggests to me, the consent is not ours; it is the British Treasury's.

May I
ask the Prime Minister a supplementary question arising out of his reply? In the event of the British Treasury authorizing a provincial government to float a loan in England, is that government, in his opinion, required to obtain the permission of the federal government before approaching the British authorities?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
So far as I recall, the
constitution of this country authorizes and permits the provinces to make loans anywhere they may desire, and on their own security. We have not endeavoured to exercise any authority over the provinces in connection with loans they may have made or may desire to make, but I think that what the hon. gentleman has in mind is that those who have money to lend have been very anxious that in some way, if money were lent to a province, they should tie the dominion up with it. Thus far they have not succeeded.

My right hon. friend will remember that during the war period provincial governments could not negotiate loans except by consent of the federal government, and I am curious to know whether the same condition holds to-day with respect to the London market.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is
no doubt aware of the fact that the War Measures Act, passed by the parliament of Canada in the emergency of war, dispossessed the provinces of much of the jurisdiction which otherwise would have been solely theirs, and we have the authority of the highest court in the land that the dominion, because of the war emergency, had certain authorities which they no longer possess. This is an instance that very clearly illustrates the different conditions that prevail. The Defence of the Realm Act in England gave to the

executive powers to make laws with respect to almost any matter about which they felt they should make laws, and the War Measures Act in this country conferred upon this parliament, and this parliament in turn upon the executive, powers much larger than could possibly be possessed except in case of national emergency, as was pointed out in the Board of Commerce case, by Lord Haldane. I do not think there is the slightest likelihood-at least I hope there is no likelihood-of any such condition again prevailing. At the moment, with the repeal of the War Measures Act, that power disappears as far as the provinces are affected.

Could the Prime Minister give us some official information on the question, and as to who is negotiating for the Canadian government.

At the conference that met at Rome a short time ago the Dominion oi Canada was represented by Colonel Vanier, secretary of the High Commissioner's office, from London, England, and Mr. McFarland of Canada. The meeting was adjourned to London, Mr. McFarland in the meantime returning to Canada. Discussions have continued between the various governments at London but no final conclusion has been arrived at. Any concessions that might be made to the Argentine by reason of the extraordinarily large crop they had would not involve Canada in the loss of any shipments that we might be able to make, for the quota we had for the year was a quota that was greater than we should be able to fill under existing probabilities. subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed from Monday, May 7, consideration of the motion of the Minister of Finance that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to resolve itself again into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Ralston.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In the
few moments I have I purpose this afternoon discussing some problems which at the present time are uppermost in the minds of those whom I have the honour to represent in this house-debt, interest, credit, cost of farm implements and price spreads. In discussing the matter of debt I purpose dealing particularly with federal debt and individual debt, individual debt in so far as it affects the agriculturist.
It is with some diffidence that I enter upon the discussion of so important a question as federal debt. According to the budget speech of the Minister of Finance, our federal debt is represented by three items. First there is the direct debt, which amounts to $2,850,000,000; then there is our indirect debt, which is largely a railway debt, with some subsidies to harbour commissions, amounting to 8990,000,000 odd; and the further railway debt, not guaranteed, amounting to $290,000,000 or in all something over 84,130,000,000
First I desire to turn my attention to the indirect debt. In a recapitulation of the indirect debt, I find that this debt is payable, part of it in Canada, part in London, part in New York, part in Canada and London, Canada and New York, and a third part, about half of it, payable at the option of the holder in Canada, New York and London, The debt, one might say, is pretty well scattered all over the lot. I find, in examining that indirect debt, the interesting fact that at the present time about 33 per cent of it bears interest at 4 per cent and under and that, according to those in authority, only about 20 to 25 per cent is held in Canada, the rest being held mostly in England and in the United States. In looking at our direct debt I find that a little over 72 per cent is payable in Canada, a little more than three per cent in Canada and New York a little more than 10 per cent in New York and the balance of about 13J per cent in London. But what I find more interesting is that in so far as a calculation can be made about the same proportion of our direct debt as I have indicated is held in Canada, New York and London. About 70 to 75 per cent
The Budget-Mr. Bowman

of our direct debt is held in Canada, about 10 to 15 per cent in the United States and about 15 per cent in London. With respect to that portion of our direct debt that is payable in London an interesting fact is that all of it bears interest at rates of four per cent and under. For the time being my purpose is to direct the attention of the house only to a consideration of that portion of our direct debt which is held in Canada, bearing in mind as I have just stated that approximately three-quarters or 70-75 per cent is so held.
I also note this other interesting fact that within the next five months we have maturing of our direct and indirect debt no less than approximately $441,000,000. A large payment falls due on June 1 next and further payments up to November and in that period of five months, we have falling due the immense sum of $441,000,000 of which
8424,000,000 is direct debt. In view of the fact that these large sums of money must be refunded during the next five or six months and also that 70 to 75 per cent out of 85 to 90 per cent is held in Canada, we must put on a huge conversion loan during the summer. In stating that I am saying what seems to me to be quite obvious. When I suggest that this conversion loan will be a success I have in mind the fact that in 1931 when conditions were much worse than they are at present we asked for $250,000,000 and -we actually had converted something over ;$634,000,000, reducing interest charges at that lime from five and a half per cent to four and [DOT]one half per cent. The next loan we made result-ted in a further reduction of interest to four per cent and during last March we were successful in placing short-term loans at 2-41 and 2-71 per cent. This indicates that from 1931 to the present time moneys have actually been loaned to the government at much lower interest rates than prevailed some three or four years ago. The loan that was placed last October has been selling recently to net the lender 3-77 per cent.
I would also point to the fact, which I think is unquestioned, that in this country the sentiment is very strongly in favour of lower rates of interest and consequently of a conversion on as large a scale as possible. I believe holders of bonds bearing interest at five or five and a half per cent realize that the rate should be lowered during these times. It seems to me that during the perilous period through which we have passed those who have been receiving five and five and a half per cent should consider it a privilege to be able to serve Canada at this time by converting those loans into bonds that would

bear a much lower rate of interest, say three and a half to four per cent. I would say further that any loss that might be sustained by a conversion of this kind would be more than counterbalanced by the speeding up of business, by the creation of better feeling in Canada, and the economic life of the country would be given an impetus that would enable those who were fortunate enough to hold bonds at a higher rate to be compensated for any loss they might suffer by reason of converting them to a lower rate. I am not unmindful of the fact that many bonds that have been issued have bearer coupons attached and there is a possibility, if a huge conversion loan were put on, that some holders- and I believe they would constitute a very small percentage

might be so unpatriotic as to send those coupons abroad in order that they might be collected in New York or London at the higher rate of interest. I am also not unmindful of the fact that this government has issued certain tax-free bonds.

speechtext:
Quite so. A previous
government has issued tax-free bonds. In looking over the record I find one issue of about $89,000,000 at five per cent which falls due on March 1, 1937, a second issue of some $236,000,000 at five and a half per cent which falls due on December 1, 1937. May I call the attention of the house to the fact that as regards the five per cent bonds, on March 1 next eighteen out of twenty payments at five per cent will have been made, and if the holders of those bonds convert them to, say, three and a half per cent, and if we presume that they held the bonds from the start, they would have realized during the whole of the twenty years an average of 4-85 per cent, which after all, is not a bad rate of interest on government-guaranteed bonds.
May I also point out with respect to the five and a half per cent issue to which I have referred, amounting to some $236,000,000, that on December 1 next seventeen full payments of interest at five and a half per cent will have been made. If the holders of those bonds found that it was to their advantage and to the advantage of Canada that they be converted into bonds bearing interest at the rate of 3i per cent, and they were so converted, the average rate for the twenty years would be 5-20 per cent; not a bad rate of interest after all for federal bonds.
It had been suggested to me in discussing this matter that if we asked for only a con-

The Budget-Mr. Bowman
version of those bonds held by Canadians we would be showing some discrimination against our own people. Possibly so. But after all, who should come to the rescue of this country if not the Canadian himself? Moreover, might I point out that if by this conversion benefit results to Canada through the saving, through lower taxation, through speeding up the business life of the country, who would reap that benefit but the Canadian, who had converted? It is not necessary for me to point out what the benefit of successful refunding would be. We would have a saving of course, the amount of which would depend on the rate of interest at which the government of the day felt the conversion should be floated and the amount converted. If the conversion loan were successful, and I have already pointed out that in times much worse than the present we succeeded in the conversion of $634,000,000, if a conversion were made of even $1,000,000,000 or $1,500,000,000 of these bonds, the saving would be very substantial. It would result in a better feeling all round. It could not then be said that the producer, the wage earner and the business man alone had taken the loss, but it would then be made clear that the bondholders had been prepared to take their share. I am satisfied in my own mind, if I am any judge at all of the feeling of the people, that such a conversion loan could be made a remarkable success. The people are for it. We have at the present time as leader of the government in this country a man who has safely piloted the ship of state through the storm of the last four years. No man in our time is more familiar with financial transactions of the magnitude such as I am discussing. With his resourcefulness, his courage, his determination, the putting through of a huge patriotic conversion loan would be I am satisfied a tremendous success. '
I have not said anything about compulsion whatsoever. Let us attempt to put this across, and after we have done so, look at the resulting picture and see what then is necessary to be done. If compulsion is then necessary let us have it, although that would be the last thing I would advocate. But after all the welfare of the state comes before that of the individual.
I have said nothing with respect to those bonds which are held abroad. I would not advocate anything with respect to them. Our credit is high in New York and London; we should keep it so. Refunding from time to time will be necessary in order to take up our obligations there. Money will be needed in
Canada for development if we are to maintain the high standard of living to which we have been accustomed in the past. So I make no suggestion whatever as to the conversion of those bonds which are held abroad. It does seem to me that at the present time our credit as a nation stands very high both in the United States and London. I am reminded of the $73,000,000 loan which went across so successfully in London. I am reminded of the fact, to which I have already drawn the attention of the house, that not one dollar of the $384,000,000 which is payable in London bears interest at a rate higher than 4 per cent. Money is plentiful over there, the rate of exchange is favourable and sentiment is strong for Canada. The prestige of this government, largely because of the prestige of its leader is high, not only in London but throughout Europe. So it seems to me not unreasonable to suppose that in the very near future money from London should be made available to Canada for current requirements at an interest rate approximating 3i to 4 per cent.
I turn to say a passing word with respect to interest on bank deposits. I understand that it is the firm opinion of the government that interest on bank deposits should be further reduced from 2J to 2 per cent; but that some difficulty lies in the way because of the fact that trust companies, which accept deposits, are under provincial jurisdiction. It does seem to me that the provinces should be prepared to cooperate with the federal government in making a further reduction in interest charges. Everything possible should be done to get more money into circulation. I shall probably refer to that again in a moment in another connection.
Then may I say a passing word with respect to individual indebtedness. I refer particularly to the indebtedness of the agriculturist, as I represent a rural community. Speaking of debts and interest I am reminded of the presentation made by the Prime Minister at the imperial conference held in Ottawa in 1932. It might be well to bear in mind that at that time the Prime Minister of Canada stressed debts, interest, credit and prices. Speaking of interest he stated on that occasion:
Interest charges represent the most important of the fixed or semi-rigid elements in our cost structure. If prices remain on their present level, such charges will constitute an intolerable or almost intolerable burden in many cases. Even if it can be borne, the fortuitous gain to the creditor of 40 to 48 per cent in general purchasing power above what he contracted for appears to be a grave injustice.
The Budget-Mr. Bowman

That was in 1932. Those same conditions exist to a considerable extent to-day, although there has been an improvement in the prices of farm products. As most members representing rural constituencies are aware, at the time when high prices of grain were prevalent in 1920, 1921 and thereabouts, farmers became indebted for very large sums of money by purchasing lands at prices above their real value and by mortgaging on a basis for which there was really little excuse, except that we are all human and we were looking to the. future in the light of the prosperity then existing. Those mortgages and debts still exist in many quarters, except where readjustments have taken place or where there have been foreclosures by the mortgage companies. Some of these companies have been fair, but many have not; the latter have insisted on the strict performance of the contract and upon payment of principal and interest in full no matter how impossible of performance that might be. As a result we have had in many cases an impossible burden of debt and interest piled upon the backs of many of the farmers who borrowed money or purchased land during the period to which I have referred. The government have indicated that they propose to bring in a measure of relief. In view of what has been said in this regard it is not for me to suggest what should be done, but may I say that those who bear this burden should be given some opportunity to compromise with their creditors so that they may make a fresh start and continue to be useful citizens adding new wealth to the country.
Now I should like to refer for a moment to the matter of credit. I represent a constituency in which, fortunately, we have had very good crops; in fact there have been no crop failures during the last twenty or twenty-five years. Last year we had the best crop we have had since 1915, so in some quarters things are not so had as they are in other parts of the west. There is one matter, however, in connection with which I think the farmer has real cause for complaint; I refer to the fact that he has not been able to obtain money to finance his operations. The bankers have practically ceased to loan money to the farmers in Manitoba, and it has become absolutely impossible to secure money from private sources. Not many years ago most lawyers practising in the smaller country towns had a certain amount of private funds to loan, but that day has passed. The mortgage companies have ceased to operate; no money can be borrowed from them. The banks have absolutely refused in, I should say, seventy-five

to ninety per cent of the cases to loan money to farmers who really should get loans. I particularly drew the attention of one or two of the bankers who appeared before the banking and commerce committee to the fact that the banks would not make advances for the purchase of binder twine, without which it is impossible for the farmer to harvest his crop. We were told in that committee that if the farmer was one to whom credit should be extended he would get it, but I am sorry to say that this has not been my experience in the northern part of Manitoba. The farmer has not been able to get money for his binder twine; he has not been able to get money to buy seed or to purchase other things needed to carry him through the season until his crop is harvested,-and that condition exists to-day. Surely there should be some means at hand whereby the farmer-I do not mean the farmer who cannot pay his debts, because there are such-who is entitled to and deserves reasonable credit should be able to obtain that credit in order to carry on his season's operations. I am quite ready to admit that I would not be prepared to suggest that the government should start a banking institution; we have had rather a weird experience in Manitoba in regard to rural credit and farm loans, but pressure should be brought to bear upon the banks and they should be told plainly that in a district such as the one I represent, which of course I think is the best constituency in Canada-

There may be those who differ, but I believe the banks should be told that in a farming constituency of that kind they should loan the farmers a reasonable amount of money in order to meet their urgent needs and to enable them to carry on until their crops are harvested.
There is another matter of tremendous importance to the agriculturists of the west; that is the cost of farm implements and machinery. Almost every member representing a rural constituency in the west will agree, I am sure, that the old binders, plows, waggons, mowers, and so on are on their last legs, because money has not been available for the purchase of new machinery, and even if it has been available the prices have been so high that it has been practically impossible for the farmer to accumulate enough money to buy the machinery he needs. I can well remember following a binder in my youth-and I could follow one then-when that machine sold for about S125. Then the price went up

to S135, and I remember that when it reached $150 to $175 the farmers thought they were paying a terrible price,-to-day, they pay about $275.

There is no need to go over there; I have noticed that all the inquiries that have been held have been started by this government.
The next question which I should like to discuss for a moment is the question of prices. In practically every rural community there is the idea that the prices the agriculturist has to pay are out of all reason when compared with the prices which he receives for his products, and when we consider what has taken place in the Stevens committee in the last few days it would seem that the primary producer is pretty well justified for some of the views he has held. May I once more refer to the presentation, bearing on the question of prices, made by the Prime Minister of Canada at the Ottawa conference of 1932:
Prices of raw materials here as elsewhere, have fallen much more rapidly than wholesale prices generally. Thus, prices of raw and partly manufactured materials have fallen 47-3 per cent since August 1929, whereas prices of fully and chiefly manufactured articles have declined only 26'0 per cent. Farm products have been particularly hard hit, the decline averaging 56-4 per cent. Wheat, the staple of the western farmer, has fallen from an average price of $1.50 per bushel in 1926 to 55 cents in June, 1932, a drop of 63-3 per cent, giving an index of 36-7 as compared with one of 70 for manufactured goods at wholesale.
Then, farther on the Prime Minister said:
I have said enough to indicate the importance which Canada is bound to place upon the solution of the problems of price instability and of unstable exchanges. In particular we believe that it is imperatively necessary to put a stop to the persistent decline in commodity prices which is paralyzing private enterprise, choking off international trade,
multiplying unemployment and social distress, and menacing the stability of our present social and economic order. We also believe it urgently desirable to encourage in every way that can be accepted as sound and practicable, a rise in prices to a height more in keeping with the fixed or highly rigid cost elements in the existing economic structures of most countries.
I say that this government has done something in the matter of price spreads and the increase of prices of primary products. Of course, the basis for the increase during the past two years in the prices of many raw products in Canada is the Ottawa agreements. I sometimes wonder where Canada would be to-day if the Ottawa agreements had not been entered into.
Perhaps it might not be amiss if we were to review one or two of the provisions in these agreements relating to hogs, cattle, lumber, copper and so on. In preparing these remarks I was interested in some statements made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) at the time the agreements were under discussion, and to compare what he then stated with what has since happened. First of all I should like to refer to hogs and hog products. At page 276 of Hansard for the year 1932-33 the leader of the opposition is reported as follows:
I come now to article 6, and I ask hon. members to see what they can make out of it in the way of definiteness. One of the faults of this whole agreement is the obscurity of the language in which it is couched, the uncertainty as to the meaning of the words and as to what their interpretation and application will be.
We find the words "obscurity" "uncertainty" and "application." Well, there is certainly no uncertainty about the agreements now. We know what the application has since been. We were told about that in the Stevens committee. Mr. McLean of the Canada Packers Limited, giving evidence before that committee stated that the increase in the price of hogs, which he attributed wholly to the Ottawa agreements, meant during the past year an additional $361)00,000 in the pockets of the farmers of Canada. Is there any obscurity or uncertainty about that? While we in Canada were receiving in the neighbourhood of eight, nine or ten cents for our hogs they were selling on the Chicago market, the place where we used to sell before the right hon. gentleman opposite was in power, for from four cents to four and a half cents per pound.

speechtext: The election may come on plenty soon enough for the hon. member who has just spoken. I notice that the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) has been laughing at my remarks about the agreements. Does he remember how hon. members from British Columbia stood in this house and said that the ten per cent preference on lumber would not help the lumber men of that province? Will they go back to their constituencies to-morrow and make the same statement? I challenge them to do so.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot find
a more appropriate expression to describe the four last years of this government's administration than that used by the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes), in the course of his budget statement. After a review of the present situation, and seeking encouragement in statistics-which a great British statesman, Disraeli, looked upon as one of the three gradations of lying-the minister praised the fortitude which the Canadian people had displayed "throughout their vicissitudes and sacrifices of these last years."
Years of sacrifices! Is truly what describes our existence under the present regime. Yet, the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) had promised happiness to all, in 1930.
If we had only to deal with these inconsiderate pledges, but, since then, how many optimistic statements have been made in parliament and elsewhere? Each year the speech from the throne informed us that business was improving and prosperity was around the corner and, each year, the budget statement revealed a fearful increase in our national debt, a deficit which has become chronic in our current transactions, new liabilities incurred and additional charges; in brief, a bankrupt balance sheet.
At a period, sir, when the people have more need to repose confidence in their ad-

ministrators, they require more than broken promises or words of hope without any foundation. They require acts to restore public confidence and safety, and this government has proved incapable of accomplishing them.
The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) and others who followed him in this debate, have made an analysis and detailed criticism of the budget. I simply wish to make a few observations and point out to the house the danger and disastrous results of the policy inaugurated and followed for the last four years, which consists in spending, and pledging Canada's credit, disproportionately to her means, without first obtaining the sanction of parliament, but simply through orders in council and, at times, under the sole signature of the Prime Minister; moreover, the danger and the consequences of a policy which favours large financial interests both local and foreign, neglects or refuses to protect the working class against every kind of exploitation, or to help the farmers and which, after, unjustly throws the burden of taxes of a ruinous administration on those who are least capable of supporting them. I intend to submit a few facts and draw from them certain conclusions which I deem of general interest.
From the very outset of his administration, the Prime Minister showed special solicitude for an old friend of his, the Canadian Pacific Railway, a solicitude which manifested itself in gifts, loans without interest and finally a guarantee on a $60.000,000 loan.
In October, 1930, shortly after the election -it was perhaps the right time to show gratitude-the government, on the authority of the Relief Act, made a present to the Canadian Pacific Railway of $863,550 and, the following year, of an additional sum of $209,196, making a total of $1,072,746, as recorded in the statement furnished by the hon. Minister of Labour, dated March 22, 1934. Yet this company was neither in difficulties or hard pressed, since in 1930, according to its balance sheet, it realized, all current and fixed charges paid, a net profit of $38,381,000, and distributed among its stockholders dividends amounting to about $38,000,000, of which $32,000,000 went to foreign holders, the preference stock being held in a proportion of about 86 per cent by foreigners.
We had no funds to carry out urgent public works, as for instance, repairs to wharves, or to continue the work begun on the Canadian National, in Montreal, which would have afforded jobs to thousands of workmen and

The Budget-Mr. Raymond
created a national wealth, but we had funds to make gifts to a friend, the Canadian Pacific Railway, and thus increase its wealth.
Yet the dividends distributed abroad by this company did not increase by one cent the purchasing power in Canada. So much for gifts.
Let us examine loans without interest. In 1932 and 1933, the government, always under the authority of the Relief Act, the blank cheque, and acting by simple order in council, loaned to the poor friend, the Canadian Pacific Railway-the distributor of magnificent dividends to foreign holders-a total amount of S2,447,222, without interest, and for an almost indefinite period. All this time, the poor Canadian Pacific Railway was accumulating, as an investment, shares of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company, an enterprise foreign to all public services.
How many industries, more humble it is true, which had never paid out large dividends, but which contributed to the livelihood of the entire population of a district where their factories were located, had to close their doors, at that time, with the results which are known. A small loan without interest, reimbursable almost at will, would have steadied and permitted them to carry on their beneficial work. How many farmers would have been saved from ruin with a similar loan. These small industries, these farmers set again on their legs would have proved a purchasing power, kept up our commerce and maintained the operations of our railways, without any other assistance. Why have railways and subsidize them if we have no freight to carry?
Let us now examine the magnificent gift of $60,000,000 made, in 1933, to this same friend, the Canadian Pacific Railway under the form of a guarantee. The Canadian Pacific Railway had borrowed $20,000,000 from the Bank of Montreal, in 1931, and $10,000,000 from the Chase National Bank Loan, in 1932, making a total of $30,000,000, maturing in 1933. Moreover, the company had notes falling due in April, May, June and November, 1934, for a total amount of $17,519,000. It was to reimburse, among others, these amounts that the government guaranteed a loan of $60,000,000 made by the banks to the Canadian Pacific Railway.
Let us investigate to what purpose served these loans, since the Prime Minister thought it too delicate a matter to inquire.
In 1931, the company borrowed $20,000,000 from the Bank of Montreal. According to its financial statement for the same year, this
company paid in dividends, on both preferred and common stocks, held, in a ratio of 85.64 per cent by foreigners, $26,190,030, while its net available returns for dividends were but $13,834,471; namely: the company was short about $13,000,000 to cover the dividend paid. Moreover, it acquired 15,858 new shares of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company. Note to what purpose had served the $20,000,000 borrowed in 1931 and reimbursed to the Bank of Montreal in 1933, thanks to the government guarantee.
The loan of $10,000,000 from the Chase National Bank Loan, in 1932, served the same purpose. During 1932, although its net returns applicable to dividends amounted to only $257,880, the company paid on its stock held by foreigners in a ratio of about 86 per cent, dividends amounting to $9,677,776, and it again acquired 14,553 new shares of Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company of a market value of about $1,500,000. Thus the $10,000,000 borrowed in 1932 and reimbursed in 1933 to the Chase National Bank Loan, thanks to the government's guarantee, had again served the same purpose, namely: to pay dividends to foreigners and facilitate the acquiring of stock in the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company.
We now come to May 30, 1933, three days after the prorogation of parliament, when following a short interview between Mr. Beatty, Sir Charles Gordon and the Prime Minister, the latter, a few hours later, under his sole signature, pledged the country's credit to the extent of $60,000,000, so as to reimburse these two loans amounting to $30,000,000, of which the bank was not then requesting payment- note well-as well as another amount of $17,519,000 maturing only in one year-again note-and this, under the plea of urgency and by virtue of "the Peace, Order and Good Government Act."

This is the kind of abuse of power which tends to rouse the people who toil and patiently bear up with the sacrifices imposed on them for the last four years, and which have the effect of discouraging and engendering distrust.
Think of the farmer's plight who, during that time, not being able to meet his liabilities, was forced to abandon his land, which he had always farmed and which afforded a livelihood to his family. subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The government boasts of borrowing at a reduced rate of interest. Why does it not reduce the rate of interest and improve the conditions of loans to farmers by virtue of the Canadian Earm Loan Act? Millions of dollars are expended to provide for those who have deserted the land, thus increasing the number of unemployed in large cities and becoming a heavy drag on the financial resources of municipalities, dominion and provincial governments. It is high time to think of applying some funds to retain on the farms those who are still there, and who instead of being a passive asset would continue to be an active one for the state. Agriculture supplies 75 per cent of our requirements. The countryside supplies water free, a home, wood as a fuel, food and even some of the clothes which are derived from the transformed agricultural products. Those are the main necessaries in life. It also contributes to increase the purchasing power and helps all the branches of economic activities which owe to agriculture the reason itself of their existence.
All agree that what is lacking to activate business is the purchasing power and that it must first come from the farming class. The farmer creates the demand. The farmer does not depend on the merchant for a livelihood but it is the latter who depends on the farmer. Cultivate the soil and factories will open their doors, workmen will find work and railways will be kept busy. Even if railways build new lines or ears, they will serve no purpose,

as long as traffic is lacking. Although agriculture should receive our first consideration, it is the most neglected of occupations.
Money or credit seems scarce to help our own people, but the government finds some for foreign shareholders of the Canadian Pacific railway or for the government of Newfoundland.
Again this guarantee of $625,000 in favour of a foreign government is an abuse of power. We thus decrease, for the benefit of others, our boiTowing power which is not unlimited, and the day will come when our borrowing power will become restricted and less advantageous.
I wish to point out another example of abuse of power which will react considerably on the farming class. It is the tax exemption enjoyed by the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power, ever since it has been under the control of the Montreal Light, Heat and Power. The Beauharnois canal was, up to September 1932, the property of the company which had built it, and it was utilized to develop electric power. The government, on the other hand, had the right to use it for navigation pur. poses. As proprietor, the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power had to pay the various municipalities its quota of taxes, because of the lands -which it had purchased and other properties it owned. Since the control has passed into the hands of the Montreal Light, Heat and Power, the government has become very obliging. It had the property of the canal transferred to it gratuitously, including bridges and certain adjacent lands, the company having -the same rights to utilize them in the operation of its water power plant, exactly as before-that is all it requires. The difference, however, is that government properties being exempt of taxes by virtue of the Municipalities Act, the company, while having practically the same rights, is now dispensed from paying taxes to the various municipalities.
The bridges are valued at more than $5,000,000, and there are about 10,000 acres which have become exempt of taxes, and the local farmers will have to portion out among themselves the taxes which the company should have paid. In one parish alone, St. Cecile, taking into account the valuation of one bridge, the five-sixths of the municipality valuation is thus exempt of taxes, so that the burden of all charges and liabilities will fall o.a the other one-sixth. This is another instance of the solicitude of the government for the large corporations to the detriment of' the rural class.

The Budget-Mr. Raymond
Favoritism does not stop there but goes so far as to allow the workman to be fleeced. Is there a more odious exploitation that the one by which the worker becomes the victim of coal importers? The government has prohibited Russian coal imports and it levies a duty on American coal. Thanks to such measures, the importers of English coal have formed a monopoly which affords them the opportunity of selling this article of necessity at an excessive price and thus make exorbitant profits. It was admitted that the profits in one year were about $400.000! Think of the profits for 1934, owing to the excessive cold we experienced; there was 25 per cent more coal consumed and prices were raised in February and again a few days ago. If there is a dealer, sir, who, because of the nature of the product he sells, should be restricted to a minimum profit for the welfare of the majority, it is certainly the importer of coal, owing to our rigorous climate which makes it an article of prime necessity. A profit of $400,000 did not seem large enough to these importers, and prices were raised this year; there was one among them who had the impudence of posing as a philantropist! Since when does Mr. Webster sell his coal simply to keep his fellow-citizens warm and prevent them from freezing to death? When shall he cease to speculate on human misery? In January and February last, there were on an average 1.275,000 people receiving the dole, so as to keep them from starvation and freezing to death; what amount did the government contribute to purchase coal for these people and thus increase the profits of the importers? How long will the government tolerate such a flagrant abuse?
The hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) ordered an investigation, by virtue of the Combines Act, which cost the country $40,451. It was held behind closed doors and the minister refused to divulge the contents of the report under the plea that it was detrimental to public interest. One helps a friend. Yet, another investigation was held in connection with the tobacco industry. The same plea was at first invoked. Finally, thanks to a by-election in South Oxford, the plea of public interest was discarded and the report was tabled in the house. However, in the case of coal, public interests seem to depend on Mr. Webster.
Surely it is not with expensive investigations, held behind closed doors, and a refusal to publish the findings, that the government will appease the public which knows that it is being fleeced. Efficient measures must be
taken. If the existing laws do not contain any appropriate remedy, let new ones be enacted. Our statutes embody very severe laws against slight offences. Thus, according to the excise act, a person found in possession of the least quantity of alcohol, on which an excise tax has not been paid-what a crime!- is guilty of an offence punishable by a fine and imprisonment, with or without hard labour for a period of one to twelve months and the government never fails to see that it is enforced. I once knew a good citizen who, during Yuletide, had purchased a quart of whisky, on which no duty had been paid. He was thrown in gaol; such cases were not left to the discretion of the magistrate.

The government provides imprisonment so as to protect the treasury, but when it is a question of protecting human life-because one dies of cold-it becomes unconcerned, in spite of the most arbitrary and extraordinary powers it possesses.
Workers are no better protected against manufacturers who on the one hand take advantage of tariff increases, enacted by the government, to maintain high prices and thus permit large dividends to be paid, while on the other hand they take advantage of unemployment to further fleece the workers by not paying them sufficient wages to provide a livelihood.
I already have had occasion to point out specific facts to the house; I shall quote others in support of them. In Valleyfield, at the Montreal Cotton Mills, a company which still pays a 7 per cent dividend to its stockholders, there are heads of families who work from six o'clock in the evening to seven o'clock in the morning, at a rate of 9 cents per hour. Twelve hours of night work, to earn SI.08. Among them, I know of one who has no choice in the matter and must provide for his wife and four children on such wages.
The government is very willing to protect manufactured goods, but it refuses to protect labour. Why did it not stipulate, when providing for tariff increases on manufactured products, that manufacturers would have to pay rational wages to the workers? The latter are entitled to wages which will provide them with a livelihood and not let them starve. It is not with such petty wages that a man can feed and clothe his family and, when winter comes, pay to Mr. Webster's company, thanks to the government's protection, an excessive price for his coal.
The Bridget-Mr. Raymond

There is a provincial statute which fixes the minimum wages for women. What happens? The Montreal Cotton Co. obliges young girls to sign a petition addressed to the minimum salary commission requesting that the company be exempted from such provision of the act, and those who refuse to sign are dismissed.
The workman is no better dealt with in the distribution of taxes and his situation is becoming worse. Certainly, taxes are needed to fill the treasury, but the least burdensome way from an economic and social angle, must be sought, and they must serve a truly useful purpose. Whence comes the greatest revenue? A perusal of the returns from taxes shows that during the fiscal year 1933-34, all taxes amounted to $271,000,000. From this amount, $61,000,000 was levied on the income tax; the balance for the most part, came from customs duties, excise taxes and that on consumption-the latter alone amounts to
S63.000,000. Of all these imposts, the largest, the most burdensome and unjust is the tax on consumption because it reaches everybody equally, without taking into account one's capacity of paying and one's circumstance. One who is in utter want is placed on the same footing as the millionaire. One who is at the head of a large family is placed on the same footing as the bachelor. It is absolutely unjust! The most equitable taxation is the one which is portioned out according to the capacity of paying. However, the latter depends on the income of the one who pays and his circumstances. The head of a family, the only bread-winner, who must provide for the livelihood of his wife and four children and who is paid by the Montreal Cotton Mills wages at the rate of $1.08 for twelve hours' night work, has certainly not the means to pay a consumption tax on articles of prime necessity.

speechtext:
Will the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Gobeil) allow me to follow up my arguments? I am not in the habit of interrupting him and I would ask him to do likewise.
When we examine what the government has done since 1930, we soon realize that no relief has been applied to the difficulties in which the country is struggling.
What have become of our resources-referred to by the Prime Minister-capable of creating work and prosperity for all? They have not melted away! Instead of work, he substituted official unemployment with all its consequences and excesses.
He spoke of the respect due to parliamentary rules, no one more than him despises them. In times of crisis, one must not close his eyes or stuff his ears, but it is befitting that measures taken or enacted be in accord with public feeling and the way to make sure of it, is to

The Budget-Mr. Maclnnis
keep in touch with it through the representatives of the people. Here, it is all jostling, one must vote on the run his measures which have hardly been introduced, otherwise it is looked upon as obstruction; parliament embarrasses him. Yet, the control exercised by parliament is the only guarantee against arbitrary rule.
There exists an atmosphere of unrest, discontent and anxiety which reaches all classes of society.
The anxiety of the farmer who depends largely on his land for livelihood since it produces most of the necessary food products, but who nevertheless feels himself crushed by various taxes, such as customs, excise, municipal imposts and other charges, rvhen it is not the expropriation through the sheriff's sale which awaits him.
Anxiety of the workman owing to the distress which prevails and awaits him if it has not already done so. Think of the unfortunate situation of the large number of people who would like to be producers, but who are condemned to involuntary or compulsory idleness, often victims of technical progress. Where production increases, more unemployment prevails. In the United States from 1919 to 1929, production increased 32 per cent while the number of workers decreased 13 per cent. At present, there are thousands who are utterly in want, with no prospect of finding work in the future; they pitifully wander through life depending entirely on public or private charity. For them, the foremost question is that of the right to work and live. Think of the situation of workmen whose only wealth are their hands and, who, victims of over ambitious manufacturers, receive insufficient or petty wages. Their home is the house of need. They are looked upon as part of a machine which serves to enrich the manufacturer.
Anxiety of the consumer with a salary hardly sufficient to live upon. Conditions of life were already hard, but they are made worse by taxing articles of prime necessity. The victims are the large families of workers who receive petty and insufficient wages. There is, at present, among the working classes, a serious unrest caused by unfair taxation. The anxiety increases at the approach of winter, when a tribute must be paid to the magnate of coal which our laws do not reach.
Among all the anxieties prevailing, there is one which should draw particularly our attention, it is the anxiety of youth, whose future, according to the expression used by His Eminence Cardinal Villeneuve, constitutes a
national problem. There are, at present, in Canada 942,000 young men between the ages of 15 and 24 in a ratio of 54 per cent in cities and 46 per cent in the countryside. What will become of them? Idleness can only have a bad effect on them. It is, however, the lot which has been assigned to most of them for the last four years. They have before their eyes thousands of unemployed and naturally wonder with uneasiness whether they will ever earn a livelihood. They need to be reassured. Does the government realize this fact? What paradox presents itself to their mind? Famine and distress side by side with abundance. If they go to the mills to obtain employment, they are told that there is no work, or that machines are doing the work, or that all places are filled. If they graduate from school, loaded with degrees and great knowledge on various subjects, whatever way they turn, the avenues are closed, all careers are filled. Yet, one must live. That is one of the sad aspects of the social problem of to-day; youth finds no employment.
Faced with all these anxieties, sir, I take the liberty to tell the government: Enough favours to friends, large corporations and foreigners; give some consideration to the farmer, worker, consumer and youth. It is not in the relief of unemployment or in the too burdensome imposts that are to be found the proper remedy to calm the anxiety of the various classes of society and inspire hope to our discouraged people.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I doubt whether there was ever a
time in Canada when Canadians took so much interest in economic and political problems as they do at the present time. Perhaps there has never been a time in the history of Canada when it was so necessary that they should do so. I know that in my own province, in every little community, in every city and town there are numbers of student economic classes held almost every day in the week.
It is my intention before I sit down to touch on what I believe to be the fundamental basis of a great part of our difficulties if not of all. However, before I come to that I wish to discuss a few other matters that are relevant to the budget.
There is nothing much in the budget this year which one need get excited about. There is nothing in it that one need strenuously oppose, and there is certainly nothing in it that can give the slightest hope to thousands of our people who have been living in misery during the last four or five years. It is a
The Budget-Mr. Maclnnis

budget which is intended to maintain the status quo. No attempt is made through it to equalize the distribution of the wealth of this country, although that is a step which in my opinion is most urgently needed at the moment.
Perhaps no other world statesman has been so much in the public eye during the last year as the President of the United States. Certainly no other government has been so energetic in its efforts to increase the purchasing power of the masses as has the government of the United States. I am not concerned now as to whether or not the steps they have taken will ultimately meet the desired end, but they surely indicate that President Roosevelt realizes the importance of a better distribution of wealth. Speaking on March 5, 1934, the first anniversary of his coming into office, he said:
Every examination I make and all the information I receive lead me to the inescapable conclusion that we must now consider immediate cooperation to secure increases of wages and shortening of hours.
That is a very different attitude from that taken by this government. No steps have been taken by this government towards that end, that is, towards the shortening of hours and the increasing of wages. It may be brought forward as an excuse that wages and hours of work come under the jurisdiction of the provincial governments, which is quite true. But it does not follow that there is nothing that this government could do'if it wished. But does it wish, or does it realize the importance of increasing purchasing power? It would seem to me it does not.
When the Prime Minister spoke at Montreal after his return from the world economic conference he said that it was not the intention of the government to follow the lead of the United States in shortening hours and increasing wages because Canada, an exporting country, could not afford to do so. I notice that just about that time the Minister of Trade and Commerce said that before President Roosevelt introduced the N.R.A. Canada had been doing the same thing for three years. I observe, however, that the minister a few days ago in Montreal made the statement that unless the manufacturers and owners of industry in this country took steps for a better distribution of wealth an N.R.A. would have to be put into effect in Canada.
In 1930 the Prime Minister was going to bring prosperity to this country by preserving the Canadian market for Canadian manufacturers. It now transpires, from the statement he made in Montreal, to which I have re-

ferred, that the Canadian manufacturer is not satisfied with the Canadian market. He must have a share in the foreign market as well and Canadian workers must toil and sweat in Canadian factories for long hours at miserable wages in order that he may get that share.
I have stated in the house on a number of occasions that the home market is not sufficient for the disposal of capitalistic production; that a foreign market is also necessary. The position which the Prime Minister now takes goes some distance toward proving my contention. I maintain that the government could use the taxing power which it has to equalize the distribution of wealth in this country; it has not made full use of its power to that end. Anyone who has followed the evidence adduced before the price spreads and mass buying committee during the last few days will realize that a few Canadians are receiving out of the wealth of the country a far greater share than that to wliich they are entitled, and that some means should be taken to ensure that that wealth is better distributed. The dominion government has the power through taxation to distribute that wealth but the government seems to be quite satisfied if it is able to meet the principal and interest on the financial obligations of the dominion. That is not wThat it was elected to do. The previous government was doing that well enough. The Prime Minister speaking for the Conservative party during the election campaign of 1930 made certain promises to the Canadian people. As those promises have been quoted in the house on numerous occasions I am not going to repeat them now but it must be kept before the people that those promises have not been fulfilled and we are not going to allow them to be forgotten by government speakers drawing attention to other things that have been done.
The Prime Minister, speaking in Ottawa as reported in the press of November 9, 1933, said:
It must be a source of great pride to every Canadian that this young country has met every obligation in the terms of the contract, at home and abroad.
During the last four years I have met a large number of Canadians and I cannot recall any whose chests swelled with pride because the government has met its financial obligations but I have met many who have bowed their heads in shame that the government has done nothing to ease the misery and want in a country so richly endowed with

The Budget-Mr. Maclnnis
the good things of life as is this one. I maintain further that the government did not meet every obligation in the terms of the contract. The contract made with the people of Canada by this government in 1930 was that it would put an end to unemployment. That contract has not been fulfilled. As I said before, the government was not elected to pay the interest on the national debt. The former Liberal government was doing that to the satisfaction of the creditors and also of the people of Canada, but it was not meeting the unemployment situation to the satisfaction of the Canadian people and that is why the present government is in office today. Before the election of 1930 and for a short time thereafter, the government had two remedies for dealing with the economic crisis facing the dominion, first, national expenditure on public works of various kinds in collaboration with the provinces and municipalities. This remedy of course was considered as being a palliative and it was soon discarded as it was found that like most palliative measures it did not palliate; that the improvement of the moment was followed by an unfavourable reaction. The real cure that the government had for the depression was increasing the tariff; tariff increases were the magic which was to drive out the demon of depression. It has always been a mystery to me why a person with the intelligence of the Prime Minister could not see the fallacy of the high tariff remedy. All that was necessary to do to realize its uselessness was to look to the great country to the south of us, a high tariff country, one with possibly the highest tariff of any in the world, where even in 1930 its relative unemployment problem was worse than ours in Canada. There were plenty of other examples besides that of the United States.
It is quite true that the United States prospered under a high tariff policy; she did up to a certain point. It is equally true that Great Britain prospered under a free trade policy, again up to a certain point. They prospered under policies which were diametrically opposed, because the conditions of the two countries were different. Great Britain prospered under free trade because she was the first in the field as a manufacturing country; she had the important essentials of a trading nation: a highly skilled working class, the most highly developed machinery of the time and plenty of coal for motive power and iron for steel and machinery. Last, but not least, as I said, before, she had an advantage over other countries by being the first in the field.
The United States prospered for very different reasons; she prospered under a high tariff because she had a large undeveloped territory, diversified natural resources and the development of the country absorbed all but a small fraction of her production until the end of the war when the country was not only developed but over-developed from a production point of view. But be it noted that neither free trade nor protection will bring back prosperity to either of those countries to-day.
In the budget there are indications, faint ones of course, that the government is losing faith in the tariff as a means of bringing back prosperity. No doubt we should be thankful for small mercies and should welcome the reductions in the tariff which are announced in the budget. The Canadian people will no doubt be grateful to the government for the reduction in the excise taxes on champagne and sparkling wines. The Minister of Finance did not tell the house whether champagne and sparkling wines would now be on the menu in the unemployment camps and included in the budgets of families on relief. Of course it may make their lot much easier to know that some people in Canada can afford to drink champagne and sparkling wines even if they themselves cannot. I noticed in speaking throughout the country that many people are worried as to who will drink the champagne and smoke the expensive cigars under socialism. I have never been able to tell them that, but I can tell them who are doing it now.
As usual in the minister's budget speeches, he ended on a hopeful note; in his position that is no doubt an appropriate thing to do, but as intelligent people we should demand some foundation for that hope. I would like to know from the minister or the government what is the cause of the depression. It is not enough to say that it is worldwide; we know that. We also know that what little improvement has taken place is also worldwide and consequently the government cannot take any credit for that. We would like to know what is responsible for the improvement, how long we may expect it to continue, what are the probabilities of the upturn in business being followed by another depression, and, more important than all, what steps the government is taking to prevent another economic collapse. Or does the government believe with the Prime Minister that we are in the grasp of a fate over which we have no control? The hope for better things is very good as far as it goes, but after all it is only a pious wish.
The Budget-Mr. Maclnnis

I maintain that before there is any permanent. improvement there must be some understanding of the factors which are essential to the functioning of the system under which we live. I maintain that we shall have to acquire an understanding of how and why our economic system functions or fails to function, and that we shall have to assume control over it; that we cannot, as we are doing to-day, leave the ordering of our economic and social life to the whims of individual interest, that if we do there will be ups and downs in our economic activities, with the consequent unnecessary suffering, as sure as day follows night.
Undoubtedly there is some reason for the slight improvement that has taken place in the economic life of the world during the last year. The present slight improvement in my opinion is due to three factors: (1) the increase in armaments and the universal preparation for war; (2) the depletion of supplies in hand of consumers' goods and the need for replacements in producers' goods, that is, new capital; and, (3) the policies of the Roosevelt administration in the United States. It will be remembered that when President Roosevelt came into office in March, 1933, the whole economic life of that country was almost paralyzed. By April there was a perceptible if small improvement, and that improvement has continued since but shows some indications now of slowing down. 'Certainly there is nothing fundamental on which we can base any measure of hope for permanent improvement. I think it has begun to be realized by many people to-day that there are certain flaws in the capitalist system itself, certain inherent faults which make it impossible of stabilization, that there are certain reasons why it must either expand or contract. In my opinion there are quite obvious reasons why the era of expansion is over and the era of contraction is now with us. Consequently there will be no permanent improvement under the present system. It is not a question of the capacity of government or even of the good intentions of government; the question is, Can the system function under the changed circumstances which now confront us?
In every organism -and machine there are vital parts or factors which are essential to the efficient functioning of that organism or machine. The same is true of a system of society. Our present system of society is breaking down because certain factors which were and are essential to its operation have become impaired. Now what are those factors? The first that I need mention is

the foreign market, that is foreign trade. The subject of foreign trade and our foreign trade policy has been mentioned in this house on a number of occasions during the last four years. In fact a certain section of the house believes that all our difficulties are due to wrong trade policies. I do not hold to that. I believe, as I said before, that in the capitalist system itself can be found the defects which -are responsible for the conditions which we find about us to-day.
I am going to try to explain this to the best of my ability from my point of view in the short time at my disposal. Capitalism is different from all other systems of production that we know anything about. It is concerned not with the production of use values but with the production of exchange values; in other words with producing goods to sell rather than to use. A country producing in this way must have a foreign market, because the producers of wealth never receive enough purchasing power in return for their labour to enable them to consume what they have produced. The owners of the means of production cannot consume the surplus because of its magnitude. It is therefore necessary in -order to dispose of this surplus to find a foreign market outside of the country of production. If that were the position only as far as Canada is concerned there would be possibly no great difficulty, but every other country in the world finds itself in the same difficult position. They also have surpluses which their own people cannot consume because they have not adequate means to buy. If they cannot buy the goods produced in their own country they certainly cannot buy what we have to sell. Here we find one of the curious contradictions of capitalism, it has many but perhaps this is the outstanding one; that is that a foreign market is absolutely essential to its existence, but it no sooner finds that market than it proceeds to destroy it.
To illustrate my point I will take two industries established in Great Britain at the beginning of the industrial revolution, cottonmanufacturing and engineering or machinemanufacturing. Great Britain was the first country to manufacture cotton with power driven machinery, and consequently the first to manufacture cotton manufacturing machinery, engines and spinning and weaving machines. Soon after Britain began to manufacture cotton with power driven machinery she had to find a market outside her borders for a considerable portion of it, not because British consumers had all the cotton they could use, because millions of the population of Great Britain to this day have never had

The Budget-Mr. Maclnnis
all the cotton cloth they have needed. But they had all the cotton goods which their wages could buy. However, the world was then the market for the products of Great Britain's cotton factories and for the labour of British workmen, because Great Britain was the only country in the world at that time engaged in machine production. But unfortunately for the British cotton manufacturer, and perhaps even more so for the British cotton operator, the British manufacturer of looms and engines also had to find an outside market for his surplus commodities, that is the looms and engines that could not be absorbed in the British market. So engines and looms were sold to other nations, who thus were not only enabled to manufacture cotton for their own needs but began to compete with Great Britain for the world market. Let me give an illustration which appeared in the press quite recently. It is headed:
British Brains and Machinery for Chinese Factories
It relates that:
Messrs. Platt Brothers, Oldham, had received large orders for textile machinery for cotton mills to be erected in South China, and a Midland firm has got the order for the electrical equipment. Mr. Harold Briggs of Oldham has been appointed' technical adviser by the Canton government, and sails for China this month. Mr. Briggs said the first mill was in course of erection and the machinery would be sent out early this year.
This export of cotton manufacturing machinery and of British capital for the development of the cotton industry in other countries has been going on for years. The result is that one-half or more of the cotton workers in Great Britain are and have been unemployed since 1920, and as far as their employment depends on the export of cotton goods they are doomed to unemployment for all time.
I was reading recently a book entitled Lancashire and the Far East. It is an history of the development of the cotton trade in India, China and Japan. It shows the effect of this development on the cotton market, over which Great Britain held a virtual monopoly for over one hundred years. I will give a few figures from this book, and I may say that all the statistics are verified as to their source. In 1913 the total export of cotton goods by Great Britain was
7.075,000,000 yards; in 1929, sixteen years later, this had shrunk to 3,765,000,000, a decrease of 47 per cent. Now let us see if we can find why this shrinkage came about. It is not necessary to tell this house that Japan is Britain's most dangerous competitor in cotton goods as well as in many other corn-74726-188
modities. In 1913, of the total exports of cotton goods to China, according to quantity, Great Britain supplied 68 per cent and Japan 23 per cent, the remainder being supplied largely by Russia and the United States. By 1925 the position was reversed, Great Britain supplying only 26 per cent and Japan 74 per cent, with Russia and the United States out of the market altogether.
I think that is sufficient to show how Great Britain, through the investment of capital in these countries, has helped to destroy the market which she needs so badly. From 1913 to 1929 Japan imported 2,000,000 yens worth of spinning and weaving machinery from England and Germany, principally spinning machinery. From 1923 on Japan did not import any weaving machinery, since she was able to supply her own requirements, and in the near future, if it is not the case already, she will be able to supply her own spinning machinery as well. Then not only will the cotton market be gone; the market for cotton manufacturing machinery will be gone as well.
Now let us come closer home. Canada is also an exporting country and is vitally interested in finding a market for wheat and other agricultural products. But Canada is interested as well in finding a market for agricultural machinery. It is held by many of our people that upon our ability to find a market for our agricultural products depends the prosperity of this country. Yet we supply the countries which we have considered as markets for our agricultural products with the machinery that will enable them to become self sufficient in regard to agriculture. Thus we destroy the markets we require so urgently. I should like to give a few figures as to our exports of agricultural machinery for 1930, which will illustrate the point I wish to make. These figures are from the Trade of Canada, 1933, issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce. During 1930 we sold harvesters or binders to thirty countries, some of whom, such as Russia, Argentine and Australia, were our competitors in the markets of the world. Others, such as France, Italy, Germany and the United Kingdom, constituted our markets for agricultural products. Here are the figures as to the sale of harvesters or binders in 1930:
