In the same year we sold ploughs and parts to sixty-two countries, to the value of

The Budget-Mr. Maclnnis

So,000,000. I think these figures are sufficient to show what is happening in every line of production. What has happened in regard to cotton has happened in regard to agriculture and almost every other industry. Is it any wonder that our exports of wheat and other agricultural products have declined? Our Liberal friends keep asserting that the only way to prosperity is through the resumption of world trade, and the other day I heard the Prime Minister make the same statement in the house. I wonder if they ever analyzed the circumstances necessary to trade or, what I would consider a better word, to exchange. The basic factor underlying exchange is the desire of one individual to get something he has not in exchange for something he has. We buy only those things we cannot produce for ourselves, or the machinery with which to produce such things. Let me illustrate this point by taking three individuals, one producing grain, the second producing fruit and the third producing dairy products. It is clear that each individual would be better off by exchanging some of the surplus of his product with each of the others for some of their surplus, but it must be obvious that if each individual, in addition to the commodity he produced at first, produced also the commodities which the others produce, there would be no incentive to and no possibility of exchange. Heretofore world trade has been largely the exchange of commodities such as I have indicated or the export and import of the machinery which would enable each country to produce a larger variety of commodities. What I have pointed out in regard to cotton and agricultural products has occurred in regard to a great many other commodities. The nations of the world are becoming more and more self-sustaining, because of the development of science and invention. In future trade will become more and more restricted to such commodities as, because of climatic conditions or the lack of natural resources, a country is unable to produce for itself.
I think the sooner we realize that fact the better it will be for us. We may rave as we please about economic nationalism, but it will not get us anywhere unless we try to understand the reasons underlying the condition we are pleased to call by that name. Capitalism expanded and became international in its outlook by reaching out and developing new countries and new areas. Now we have come to the point where there are no further new countries or new areas to be developed-or

possibly exploited would be a better word- and the capitalists of the world are forced, as a matter of self preservation, to try and secure to themselves the home market. Right Hon. Walter E. Elliot, British Minister of Agriculture, put the case very neatly in a speech he made some little time ago, in which he referred to the three stages in our development during the last one hundred and fifty years or so. He said:
But these factors, the power of science to make anything anywhere, the determination of men to try everything everywhere, and a growing doubt as to whether foreign loans in many parts of the world are not simply free gifts which we should do as well to keep for ourselves, have produced and are producing a change so fundamental in our outlook that it might almost be described as the third stage of the industrial revolution. The first stage was, so to speak, the drilling of a borehole and the tapping of a great subterranean source of power by the people who made this venture. The second, which we have just lived through, was the piping off of that power to undeveloped nations as capital development, financed by unrepaid loans.
That is, the sending of capital into new areas.
The third stage is the check and flood-back as the boreholes in other countries strike oil in their turn, and the pipes begin to fill tip from the far end also.
I think that is a very clear picture of what has happened in the world markets during the last few years. In my opinion there is no doubt that the foreign market is fast disappearing, never to return as we once knew it. As the British Minister of Agriculture points out, this is the inevitable effect of the development made possible by science and invention.
And that is not all. The capitalists, in their endeavour to hold the dwindling foreign market, are destroying the home market as well. This is being done by reducing wages, increasing the hours of work, increasing the intensity of labour, and by the greater use of labour-displacing machinery. They call it reducing the cost of production, and it is done to increase profits, of course. But it is also done in order to enable them to compete for a share in the fast dwindling world market. Let us see how it works. If the manufacturer of cotton goods reduces his production costs in the way I have mentioned he may be enabled better to meet competition in the world market, but it further reduces the home market because the employees affected have lost buying power and consequently are less able to buy the other goods such as food, furniture and clothing which are produced at home.

The Budget-Mr. Belec
It also reduces the world market, as Canada's home market is the foreign market, or at least part of the foreign market for all other countries. This is an inevitable and inescapable consequence of the system of production under which we operate.
The next factor necessary to the efficient working of a capitalistic system is the ever-extending field for development and the investment of new capital. I say "the ever extending field" because in the ordinary capitalistic state the capital investment increases yearly by the reinvestment of part of the profits of the preceding year. In fact, the purpose of capitalist production, as I have said before, is the production of new capital which is invested for the purpose of producing more capital values.
I have some figures before me taken from the Canada Year Book, concerning manufacturing in Canada, showing that invested capital increased from 178,000,000 in 1871 to $5,093,000,000 in 1929. If hon. members would compare the increase in wages with the increase in capital they would find that salaries and wages did not keep pace with capital invested. In the same period wages increased from $40,000,000 in 1871 to $813,000,000 in 1929. These figures are the total amounts paid in wages and salaries. Outside of the market for government bonds and debentures there is no great opening to-day for the investment of new capital. In 1930 corporation bonds to the value of $146,303,000 were sold in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with great pleasure that I extend my congratulations to the Minister of Finance for the exceedingly able manner in which he presented the budget to the house. It is a matter of great satisfaction to learn that in the twelve months period ending March 31 last, exports of Canadian produce increased by $105,500,000, or 22 per cent over the same period last year. Imports, advancing less 74726-188J
rapidly at first but showing greater gains in recent months, increased by $27,300,000 or 7 per cent. The improvement in the aggregate trade was $132,000,000 over the same period last year, or 15 per cent. The total trade exceeded one billion dollars.
The beneficial effects of the empire trade agreements are shown in the expansion of intra-empire trade. In the eleven months period ending February 28 of the present year exports from Canada to the United Kingdom, our largest market, increased by 20 per cent, accounting for more than half of the increase of sales abroad. Exports to Australia increased by 54 per cent, to British India by 45 per cent, to British South Africa by 72 per cent and to New Zealand by 6 per cent. Statistics of the United Kingdom show that whereas in 1931 imports from Canada represented 3'8 per cent of the total purchases from abroad, in 1933, Canadian products represented 6-9 per cent of the total. Prominent among the commodities showing increased exports to the United Kingdom were planks and boards, apples, meats, copper and other metals, and cattle.
It is a matter of pride to all Canadians to remember that Canada, with a population slightly over ten millions of people, is the fifth trading nation of the world. At this time, when world recovery is slow, our country has increased its exports and is slowly but surely emerging from depression to prosperity. I am sure that the next year will continue to show a marked improvement in conditions.
In the budget it will be noticed that the dominion treasury has stood the brunt of depressed conditions in all parts of the country, and especially in the western provinces. A total of $36,000,000 was expended in the last fiscal year for relief measures. The budget discloses that the expenditures made since 1930 by the dominion on unemployment relief have reached $115,500,000, to which may be added the cost of the wheat bonus in 1931, amounting to $12,700,000 and $2,400,000 advanced for employment in railway shops, a total of $136,600,000
It is these relief expenditures and public works expenditures that I want to discuss, especially in their relation to the county of Pontiac The Department of Labour has kindly sent me a statement showing dominion contributions to relief expenditures in Pontiac -in Temiskaming, Abitibi, and old Pontiac These were as follows:

Last year I advocated the construction of the Sheenboro highway and could have secured an appropriation from the dominion government, but the authorities at Quebec would not join with us in building the road which would be a new means of communication with the north country. Besides it would have provided much needed work. I should like to quote a statement made on March 22 by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) in reply to the hon. member for North Timiskaming (Mr. Bradette). This appears on page 1724 of Hansard and is as follows:
Might I interrupt a moment? As far as the trans-Canada highway is concerned I do not think the hon. member wants to be understood as saying that in his judgment the trans-Canada highway should go up to Senneterre and out to Manitoba in that direction. And I do not think he means that the road from Sheenboro to connect with Kipawa in Quebec is not being built because of any neglect on the part of the dominion government, because the fact is we have received no schedule and no request for any contribution to that road which would connect with the Ontario roads passing through Rouyn down to Ottawa and Montreal. The Sheenboro-ICipawa-Ville Marie road is the one break which has necessitated the people in the north end of Pontiac and the Rouyn mining country coming down to Montreal and Toronto by the Ferguson highway in Ontario. I do not think the hon. member wants to be understood as meaning that the province

The Ferguson highway has been the outlet to the front, both Toronto and Montreal, for all of that north part of Pontiac to the present time, and still is as far as vehicular and motor traffic is concerned.

I take this opportunity of congratulating the Minister of Finance upon cutting in half the tax on sugar. This tax, which was two cents per pound has been cut to one cent, and I hope the state of the treasury will permit the minister to abolish the tax next year. All taxes are unpopular, but this levy has aroused the ire of the housewife who uses a great deal of sugar at preserving time.
It gives me the greatest pleasure and satisfaction to declare that I am proud to support a government which has introduced such measures as the marketing bill, the Bank of Canada bill and the proposed works program. All of these things will prove to be advantageous to our country. The marketing bill will be of great advantage to agriculture because it is designed to increase the prices of farm products by facilitating the efficient and profitable marketing of live stock and all other produce of the farm.
I have not sufficient time, Mr. Speaker, to go into the back to the land movement thoroughly. I will say that I have visited every part of my riding every summer and particularly the back to the land settlements. There are 398 families who have gone back to the land in the Abitibi district and 351 families in the Timiskaming district. They are happy because they are industrious and hard-working. Both, I am glad to say, will be fine settlements. Those people have gone in with the determination to make good and what they have accomplished in such a short time would surprise you. Recently I visited the new settlement at Laferte and there I found that a fine sturdy lot of settlers had located and were busy finding new homes in Pontiac county. Of course, there are criticisms I could make as to the way in which the Quebec government has administered these settlements, but I hope that the authorities at Quebec will deal with these

The Budget-Mr. Belee
complaints as this is entirely a provincial matter, and out of my hands. I might say that too much money has been spent on transporting these new settlers, but as the administration of the settlements rests squarely upon the Quebec government I can do nothing but voice these complaints, hoping that the authorities at Quebec will step in and correct them.
I want also, Mr. Speaker, to congratulate the Minister of Finance on his words in the budget in which he indicates there is to be a lowering of interest rates. Interest rates have proven to be a heavy burden to the farmer. Now I am glad to say that the government proposes to bring down legislation designed to provide machinery whereby farmers who find themselves unable to pay the fixed charges on their outstanding debts will be able by an expeditious and inexpensive process to work out compromises with their creditors and to obtain new working capital. The guiding principle of this legislation will be to secure for the farmer a simplified debt structure reduced in size to a point where the carrying charges will be within the capacity of farm enterprise to pay. This will involve some concessions on the part of creditors, as outlined by the Minister of Finance, but these will be more than outweighed by the advantages which will follow as a result of retaining the farmer as a willing and effective producer. As the Minister of Finance points out, the release of economic energy so produced and the substitution of hope and goodwill for despondency and discontent which are now prevalent in certain parts of our country should result in a real gain to our whole domestic economy.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to tell something of the riches of the county which I have the honour to represent. Pontiac county is the largest gold-producing county in the province of Quebec. In 1924, 1925, and 1926 the molybdenite mines produced a total of $30,855.
The next year, 1927, the production increased to $40,000. Then in the northwest section of the county, Rouyn and other parts, there were great gold and copper discoveries. To illustrate the mineral riches of the county I will simply give the production figures:

1929		 10,215,791
1930		 11,339,902
The reason 1930 has such a high figure is - the increased price of copper.
1931		 $9,388,200
1932		 9,509,199
1933		 9,646,281

Thus, Mr. Speaker, you will see that since 1924 Pontiac county produced $55,667,533 in new mineral wealth. Great mines like Nor-anda, Siscoe, Treadwell, Big Ben, Beattie, Cadillac, which I visited last summer, were working three shifts. Men were at work; men were happy. There was no depression in that area. Further, these mines were stabilizing conditions in the depression. They were stimulating other branches of industry by their purchases of materials and were a boon to the agriculturist. I am glad that the government has modified the tax on gold, and I am sure that the industry is appreciative of the fact.
On the whole I am proud to represent such a fine county as Pontiac with its great people and richly diversified resources. I have been in the House of Commons just over three years and believe that I have done my duty. I am proud to support such a strong leader as the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett whose policies saved Canada in the depression.

To summarize, the government could levy $78,000,000 more on the income tax; $50,000,000 on gasoline; $15,000,000 on coal; $25,000,000 on stocks sold on the exchange, which would make a grand total of $168,000,000; while those who would pay that amount would in no way be the poorer, because they have the means to do so. This amount could have helped the government to suppress all the taxes levied on the farming and working classes, ever since they are in office.
There are many other trusts in this country from which the government could levy taxes in order to relieve the worker and farmer. All suggestions, sir, coming from the opposition which might improve our financial situation and relieve the people from overtaxation, does not meet the wishes of this government which has its own way of drawing the last penny of poor people and protecting a small group of millionaires who control the trusts on gasoline, coal, water powers and tobacco and many others, to the detriment of the people.
The Canadian people had a right to expect that the budget of 1934 would show some improvement, they had a right to expect that the prime minister would reduce taxation which so heavily burdens the poor, the workmen and farmers. The Prime Minister should have read what his predecessors have written or stated and the views of great financiers on high protection. The following are a few excerpts:
Toronto, January 24, 1933.
Sir Robert Borden, speaking in Toronto, last evening, insisted on the necessity of a greater freedom in trade relations throughout the world.
And to obtain a greater freedom in our trade relations, we must lower our tariff barriers.
Toronto, March 25, 1934.
The Hon. Mr. Meighen, former Prime Minister, speaking in Toronto:
The country's salvation demands a remedy for unemployment. People who set aside their savings in order to speculate should be made to bear the taxes.
This former prime minister would no doubt approve of the tax which I suggested. Those who speculate in stocks should be made to pay instead of the workman.
Saskatoon
Sir Henry Drayton, Chairman of the Financial Committee of the Board of Trade,

suggested in his speech to reduce expenditure and taxes so as to accelerate the movement of economic restoration.
April 11, 1934.
The following is what Mr. S. H. Logan, Director of the Canadian Bank of Commerce, stated:
The high tariffs of importing countries were responsible for the crisis in this country.
February 21, 1934.
Sir Arthur Balfour of Sheffield, London:
That protection barriers constitute a greater threat to the peace of the world than the building of war ships.
This should make the protectionists of this country pause.
As you may judge, sir, by all these statements, high protection is a thing of the past and the government must, to relieve the crisis, entirely change its policy.
What remedy does this year's budget propose so as to relieve unemployment and reduce the cost of living? The government reduced by one cent the tax on sugar and cigarette tubes, a tax which had been in force for one year only, and the most unjust one that ever was levied by a government. If the government -tax on sugar has been reduced it is not because its finances have improved-the national debt has increased by $135,000,000-but because of the protests of the Liberal party and the public.
Let us examine the tax on hops and beer. The government has made some changes in connection with the 3 cents tax on hops. After suppressing the 12i cents tax per gallon on beer, they increased the tax on hops to 7i cents. They contend that the returns will be as large while the work of officials of the department will be greatly lessened. I have been informed that the government intend to levy a further tax on the people by increasing the tax on hops. Most of our families that bake their own bread use hops and a number of our workmen and farmers who have not the means to purchase beer brewed by trusts, make their own beer and use hops. If the government expect to levy as large a revenue, by this new tax on hops they will be protecting the beer trust to the detriment of the working and farming classes.
Since this government has been in office, it has yearly increased the customs tariff. Our prime minister should realize that high protection has not been a success, because, since he is at the helm of affairs, the country's debt has increased over $500,000,000, namely, an increase of $2 per capita, yearly. Such is the result of the Bennett high protection.
The government could have ended the crisis by accepting the solution which my colleague,

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENTS RESPECTING NATIONALITY OF WOMEN

speechtext:
Mr. J. L. BROWN (Lisgar) moved the second reading of Bill No. 31, to amend the Naturalization Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the bill to which I am now asking that second reading be given has been on the order paper since early in the session, and I may say that it was brought forward at the request of some of the women's organizations in Canada. Since it appeared on the order paper I have received many communications from women in all parts of the dominion expressing their sympathy with the purpose of this amendment. In late years we have done a great deal towards giving women equality of status with men in almost all walks of life. They can sit in the House of Commons; it has been decided that under the law they are persons who can sit in the Senate, and in many other ways we have given them the privileges and rights that have been given the men. Many of the women still feel that in this matter of naturalization, however, they are not occupying the status they would like to occupy. It is true that much has been done, and many of the actions that have been taken have met with hearty approval. I might refer to the fact that in 1931 the Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) brought in a bill, which passed this house, giving women the privilege of retaining their British nationality after marriage unless at that time they took the nationality of their husbands, and I should like to express on behalf of the women and the people of Canada generally an appreciation of the fact that the regulations concerning the naturalization of women have been somewhat modified, particularly in the matter of expense. At the same time, however, there is a feeling on the part of many that our laws have not gone as far as they might in recognizing the rights of women to naturalization in their own right.
It is not my intention to occupy a great deal of time in speaking on this bill to-night, since I know the mind of the minister and would like to give him full opportunity to express his attitude. I intend to make my remarks veiy brief, but I should like to bring to the notice of the house the fact that under existing laws cases still arise which entail a good deal of hardship and confusion. Just a few days ago I received a letter from a firm of solicitors in Toronto which I think I should read, without giving the names:
We note that you introduced Bill No. 31, an act to amend the Naturalization Act. upon March 12th. 1934. and have been awaiting news of the passage of this 'bill through parliament.
A young Dane applied through us for naturalization papers last October, subsequently married on December 16th last and expects to receive his certificate of naturalization within the next few weeks. Upon receiving his certificate he proposes to take his wife to Denmark for a short visit.
Should your bill be passed and become effective before the 16th of June, 1934, we feel

Naturalization Act-Mr. Brown
that the young woman may safely consider herself to have retained her British nationality, despite her marriage to a man who was, at the time of such marriage, an alien. Otherwise, the determination as to her status of nationality involves several complicated problems in private international law.
Accordingly, we should be pleased if you could inform us whether your measure is likely to become effective by June 16th, as we must advise our client in what steps she will need to take to enable her to pass through Europe unhampered.
That is just one illustration, and I believe there are numerous cases in which a great deal of confusion and perhaps actual hardship is experienced because of the present law.
Another matter has been brought to my attention, and the papers in reference to it were just placed in my hands as this bill was called. I have not had an opportunity of reading them, but as I understand it this is the situation: If I am correctly informed our department has refused to grant naturalization certificates to people from Switzerland because the Swiss government is not willing to release them from their allegiance to their own country. Perhaps I am not stating the case correctly but, as I have said, these documents were placed in my hands just a few moments ago by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Hanson), who was talking with me some little time ago about the matter.

It does seem only fair and reasonable, however, that we should grant naturalization to all applicants who conform to our laws, and it is open to question as to just how far we should allow our laws to be governed by the laws of other countries. It may be that in some cases it would mean dual nationality, which may be objectionable from some points of view, but at the same time I think this is a matter that should be considered.
I have here another extract which I should like to read to show that the women of the empire as well as those of Canada are taking a very active interest in this question and are asking that Canada give a lead to the empire in matters of this kind:
Dominion women who want Canada to take the initiative in legislation providing that a married woman should' have her own nationality and not be required to adopt the [Mr. Brown. 1
nationality of the man whose wife she has become, waited on the High Commissioner at Canada House the other day.
They urged that one of the dominions- Canada for preference-should take the first step towards producing agreement between all parts of the empire, since opposition to the reform seemed now to consist of stressing the difficulty of securing such unanimity.
British women, it was alleged, had lost the right to keep their own nationality after marriage by legislation in 1870. Before that date British women who married foreigners remained British.
As a result of recent legislation in Canada and the United Kingdom there was now no longer uniformity in the empire, a married woman in some cases being regarded as British in one place but not in another. The deputation also urged that the Hague Nationality Convention, which accepted the principle of the dependence of the nationality of the wife on that of the husband, should not be ratified.
Mr. G. Howard Ferguson thanked the deputation for putting their views before him and undertook to transmit them to Ottawa.
I am perfectly aware of many of the difficulties which may confront us before we could reach a final solution of this matter. Some progress has been made, but that it has not been made fast enough to satisfy the desires of our people is I believe hardly open to question. The women who asked me to bring this matter before the house were very insistent with regard to it, and I Should like to have the matter considered by the house.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. H. CAHAN (Secretary of State):
subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENTS RESPECTING NATIONALITY OF WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member has observed, this matter is surrounded with many difficulties, one or two of which in his short statement he has emphasized. For more than a century in Canada we have from time to time had difficulties with regard to the naturalization of aliens in this country. Under the laws of Upper Canada, of Lower Canada, and again under the laws of United Canada after 1840 down to 1867, and again from 1867 to 1914, this matter from time to time has been under the consideration of successive legislatures. But until 1914 in none of the provinces of Canada, old or new, had the parliaments or legislatures the legislative authority to grant a certificate of naturalization to an alien which would be in force beyond the confines of Canada, whether the old provinces of Canada or the more recent Dominion of Canada as we have known it since 1867. To grant to an alien a certificate of naturalization that is not recognized by other British dominions or by the United Kingdom on one hand or by any foreign power on the other has served under the laws which have heretofore existed to place such naturalized Canadian under insurmountable difficulties the moment he passes

Naturalization Act-Mr. Cahan
the three mile limit of Canada. In fact the condition reached a crisis in Canada at about the time of the Franco-German war. Many aliens had received naturalization certificates in Canada making them British subjects in Canada, but the moment they passed outside Canadian borders they were not recognized as British subjects in any part of the British Empire or in any other part of the world. So that in 1873 the parliament of Canada, after reciting the grievances which resulted from other parts of the empire not recognizing certificates of naturalization made in any other part of the empire, and which resulted from foreign countries refusing to recognize those certificates of naturalization, passed a resolution. The text of the resolution was as follows:
Resolved that an humble address be presented to Her Majesty setting forth the aforesaid grievance and praying that Her Majesty will be graciously pleased to take such steps as may be necessary for the redress of the same, by the negotiation of naturalization treaties between Great Britain and the German and other foreign states, so that legally naturalized foreigners in Canada may not hereafter be subjected to the disabilities of a divided allegiance, but be entitled to all the rights, privileges and protection of British subjects in every part of the world, and in as full a measure as if they had been subjects of Great Britain by birth.
This address was engrossed and dispatched to Her Majesty. I have not the time to enter into the subsequent political discussion or the decisions of the British courts with respect to colonial naturalization. But it was clearly decided in the British courts time and again up to and including the time of the recent great war that no force or effect beyond the territorial limits of a dominion or of a colony or a possession of Great Britain could be given to its naturalization act, so long as section 16 of the imperial act of 1870 remained in force. And at the present time when those citizens or subjects of foreign states who, prior to 1915, received naturalization certificates in Canada pass beyond the confines of Canada and enter any other part of the British dominions, they are not regarded as British subjects. If they enter any European state, and particularly the state or states of which they were subjects or citizens prior to their naturalization here, their Canadian certificate of naturalization is not recognized, and from time to time we are met with cases of such citizens going abroad possessing the old form of certificate of naturalization, being arrested, compelled to do military duty and subject to pains and penalties because they have not returned to their native country to perform military services and other civic
duties. Under our law, however, there is a provision whereby they may obtain a new naturalization certificate from the Secretary of State of Canada giving them all the rights of British subjects in every part of the British dominions. But it is impossible- although I urge it from week to week and from year to year-to impress upon them the necessity of applying for such certificates, known as imperial certificates.
This matter of our naturalized citizens or subjects having no rights as British subjects beyond the confines of Canada was a subject very dear to the heart of the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier. The matter was discussed at the colonial conference of 1902, again at the imperial conference of 1907 and again at the imperial conference of 1911, at which the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the then Prime Minister, represented Canada. At the conference in 1911 Sir Wilfrid urged that an imperial act should be so framed and enacted so as to enable each self governing dominion to adopt it, and thus bring the naturalization laws of the United Kingdom and of the several dominions into complete conformity He insisted that imperial nationality should be world wide and uniform, each dominion being left free to grant local nationalities as heretofore on such terms as its legislature should think fit. It is unnecessary for me to enter into a full consideration of what took place at the conference of 1911, but the result was that in 1914 the parliament of the United Kingdom passed what is known as the Naturalization and Status of Aliens Act, and in the same year that act was adopted by the parliament of Canada. It has been adopted also by Australia, South Africa and New Zealand. So that so far as the empire is concerned, any British subject receiving a certificate of naturalization in Canada under that act is a British subject throughout the whole of the British Empire. Those who received certificates under the acts prior to 1914 were not British subjects once they had passed beyond the confines of the dominion in which they had received their certificate.
A number of cases arose during the late war which those lawyers who desire to study the question will find exceedingly interesting. One was the case of a German who went to Australia early in life and received a certificate of naturalization in that country prior to 1914. After the outbreak of the war he went to England and was arrested as a German subject who had not reported to the police under the laws then in force in the United Kingdom. The courts of England decided that having been naturalized under the old

Naturalization Act-Mr. Cahan
acts prior to 1914 he was not a British subject once he went beyond the confines of Australia. He was imprisoned and visited with severe penalties for not reporting. This case is reported in Regina vs. Francis, ex parte Mark-wald, 1918, 1 King's Bench, 617. It again came before the courts and is reported in Markwald vs. Attorney General, 1920, Court of Appeal, 1 Chancery, 349. Another case arose in British Honduras, to which a man, I think a German, had come with his father at an early age. His father became naturalized and he himself became a naturalized British subject. Later on he rose quite high in the legislative council of that colony and subsequently became acting governor. For some reason or other one of the central American states had some criticism to make of his official acts as governor and when he left the confines of the colony he was arrested. The British government refused to intervene on the ground that he was a British subject only when within the confines of that colony.
It has become very important in our efforts to solve these various difficulties that we should conform to the agreements made at the conference of 1911 and reaffirmed at every imperial conference since that date. It was then agreed that changes in naturalization laws should not be made by any dominion or by the parliament of the United Kingdom without the general consent of the other self governing dominions, so that a British subjest in one dominion might thereafter be a British subject in the other dominions. That convention has been carefully adhered to. The matter was brought up at subsequent imperial conferences and at the last imperial conference held in 1930 it was again affirmed. I quote from the report:
That, if any changes are desired in the existing requirements for the common status, provision should be made for the maintenance of the common status, and the changes should only be introduced (in accordance with present practice) after consultation and agreement among the several members of the commonwealth.
It was in accord with the agreement reached at that conference that I had the honour in 1931 of introducing an amendment to the Naturalization Act of Canada. This amendment conferred much larger privileges upon married women in Canada who had married foreigners, in certain cases, and to others who were aliens but who had married British subjects in Canada or who had been naturalized by certificates of naturalization issued in this country. That bill of 1931 subsequently became law and was adopted ver-

batim by the parliament of Great Britain at a recent session and is now the law of the United Kingdom as well. We have proceeded in conformity with that understanding because it appears to be useless and vain to maike an alien a British subject in Canada when he will not be recognized as a British subject in the other dominions.
There is another phase to the question. Under the act of 1914 we could grant certificates of naturalization to alien men or women, but such a certificate granted to a Swiss subject or a subject of Czechoslovakia or of nearly all the other European states without their consent is not of great value. Such a certificate may lead that naturalized British subject into great trouble if he proceeds beyond the confines of this country and visits the state of which he was a former citizen or subject. Therefore to this day when we grant certificates of naturalization to the citizens or subjects of certain states we ask those states to release the particular applicant from his allegiance to the state of which he was a former citizen or subject Otherwise, we have to bring to his notice and impress upon him that when he goes beyond the confines of this country his status as a British subject will not be recognized by the state of which he was a former citizen or subject and may not be recognized by many other European states.

speechtext:
I should have said, going
ouside the confines of Canada into a country other than a British country.
This matter has now again come up for careful consideration. We recognize that a statute passed by the parliament of Canada under which a citizen or subject of a foreign country becomes a British subject in Canada is really ineffective when it comes into opposition with the statutory law of Switzerland, of Czechoslovakia or of a number of other states which I could mention, which declare that unless released from his original nationality, the certificate of naturalization as a British subject will not be recognized in that country. An effort was made by the late administration to avoid the difficulties which arose out of this dual or divided allegiance, by seeking to secure the acquiescence or recognition by foreign states of the granting of certificates of naturalization as British subjects in any part of the British Empire.

Naturalization Act-Mr. Cahan
This question came before the imperial conference of 1926 and was then referred to an expert committee on interimperial relations. That committee met in October, 1929, and the Minister of Justice in the late administration, the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) , represented Canada on the committee. That committee, after a thorough investigation of all the interrelations of this question, deferred definite action in view of the necessity of obtaining international cooperation and consent, and also in view of the fact that a conference had been called at the Hague for the codification of international law and the knowledge that this subject would then be considered by the representatives of all the nations at that conference at the Hague. That conference met in March and April, 1930, under the auspices of the League of Nations, and Canada, which was represented by a delegate appointed by the late government, became one of the signatories to that convention, which is known as the Hague Convention.
That convention was subject to ratification by the signatory states and it was provided that ratifications should be deposited with the secretariat of the League of Nations. With regard to the nationality of married women this Hague convention provided as follows:
Article 8
If the national law of the wife causes her to lose her nationality on marriage with a foreigner, this consequence shall be conditional on her acquiring the nationality of the husband.
Article 9
If the national law of the wife causes her to lose her nationality upon a change in the nationality of her husband occurring during marriage, this consequence shall be conditional on her acquiring her husband's new nationality.
Article 10
Naturalization of the husband during marriage shall not involve a change in the nationality of the wife except with her consent.
Article 11
The wife who, under the law of her country, lost her nationality on marriage shall not recover it after the dissolution of the marriage except on her own application and in accordance with the law of that country. If she does recover it, she shall lose the nationality which she acquired by reason of the marriage.
At that session at the Hague, during two long months, very definite differences of opinion were expressed by the representatives of the several nations. In fact, the conference was almost equally divided for and against permitting married women to acquire a separate and distinct nationality from the nationality of the husband, and the articles which I have read were tentatively adopted,
subject to ratification, as the largest measure of agreement that could be reached by the nations there represented. Although that convention was signed by a representative of the late government, events ensued in 1930 which prevented the government of the right hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) from ratifying it. It was therefore brought again to the attention of the imperial conference of 1930, and by common consent of the British dominions there represented in that conference if was agreed that legislation should be introduced by the several dominions to carry that convention into effect. The bill of 1931 Which I had the honour of introducing has carried the Hague convention into effect to the full extent at which an agreement was reached at that convention, and Great Britain, as I have said, has enacted a similar measure, with the result that both Great Britain and Canada, together on the same day, have deposited ratifications of these several sections of the Hague convention which I have read.
Now that Hague convention is likely to sit again within a short time. There is provision whereby it may be convened again in January, 1936, as provided in article 27 of that convention, at the request of nine states, members of the League of Nations, who have ratified the convention; and it is certainly to be hoped that when that Hague convention resumes its session in 1936, if there are nine states who have ratified it, there will be further consideration of the entire subject. And in so far as the British dominions agree, and foreign states acquiesce, we shall feel that it is competent for us to extend the rights and privileges which are desired by many women throughout the country.
My hon. friend's bill has been drawn under one or two misapprehensions, because an unmarried woman has exactly the same right as a man, whether married or not, with respect to the obtaining of naturalization. But the government feel that in view of the attitude taken by their predecessors, in view of the long line of consistent policy which has developed during the last century, now, when for the first time we have reached agreement to a certain extent with the British dominions as to the rights and privileges of British subjects throughout the empire, now when we have reached with certain states in Europe a consensus of opinion with regard to the rights and privileges which should be granted by European states as well as our own to women, it is inadvisable for this parliament to disrupt that continuity of progress and policy and to revert again to the state of

Naturalization Act- Mr. Butcher
embarrassment and difficulty with which this country had been confronted for nearly a century.
There are very few states indeed which recognizes that a Canadian woman, a British subject, who marries an alien of a foreign state can retain her British nationality after such marriage, because by the law of most states she thereby becomes a citizen or subject of the foreign state-Czechoslovakian, the Swiss, and a number of others. And until we can reach an agreement whereby naturalization in this country is recognized by those foreign states, in the case of our naturalization of their citizens, we should, we think, proceed very warily and very cautiously. Therefore I feel that this government has consistently followed the policy laid down by its predecessors running back to the decision of Sir Wilfrid L aurier at the conference of 1911.
The subject is a very complicated and difficult one. Throughout the year several hundreds of letters a week reach my office dealing with the complicated conditions to which the hon. member who has moved the second reading of this bill has referred. We endeavour to solve those difficulties as best we can, but there is no solution which we can devise in respect of an alien who has become naturalized in this country going abroad unless he is recognized as a British subject by the state of which he was formerly a citizen. I think this matter will be settled perhaps within a few years; I hope it will be settled at the next assembly at the Hague. I did my best when the matter was brought up at the assembly of the League of Nations at which I had the honour of representing this country, but it was then impossible to obtain the consent of any large number of foreign states to our going further than we have gone in following out the decision of the imperial conference of 1930 and the Hague convention of the same year.
I trust the hon. gentleman, after he has elicited the views of the house, will feel disposed to withdraw the bill on its second reading and leave to this government or successive governments ample elbow room in working out these difficulties which are very grievous and embarrassing.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at 6 o'clock, I was discussing a resolution that my colleague and friend, the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough introduced in the house in 1933 and which, had it been adopted, would have greatly helped the farming class. This resolution was again introduced this year, and is as follows:
Trade With The United States
Proposed reciprocal arrangement for exchange of natural products.
That in the opinion of this house, it is expedient that the government of Canada reopen negotiations with the government of the United States of America with a view of bringing about a satisfactory reciprocal trade arrangement between Canada and the United States, whereby the natural products of Canada, that is the products of the sea, the
farm, the mines and the forests, and including fish, lumber, wheat, cattle, etc. should have free entry into the United States, in exchange for the admission of certain goods from the United States of America, which in the interests of both countries may be admitted into Canada, free from customs tariffs.
The following is the Prime Minister's reply to the resolution, on February 19, 1934.
Right Hon. Mr. Bennett: I move seconded by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes):
That all the words after the word "that" in the said' resolution be struck out and the following substituted therefor: -
"on the 1st day of May, 1933, the Prime Minister informed this house that the governments of Canada and the United States of America had agreed to begin a search for means to increase the exchange of commodities between the two countries and thereby promote not only economic betterment on the North American continent but also the general improvement of world conditions, and while no trade agreement between the two countries has yet been arrived at, this house approves of the government continuing their efforts to that end."
It would have been preferable for the Prime Minister to state immediately that he did not desire to sign any treaty with the United States and that he intended to allow our representative, at Washington to idle away his time. The latter costs the country nearly $100,000. Had he had any intention to sign a treaty with the United States, he certainly had time to do so since he opened negotiations with them. Our farmers would have benefited this year by such a trade agreement, especially as to maple sugar, which sold in Canada, in 1934, 6 cents per pound less than in the United States. In fact all farm products mentioned in the resolution of the hon. member for Antigonish-Guys-borough would have benefited.
However, it is contrary to the Prime Minister's policy to lower the tariff. All for Great Britain, whether it suits us or not makes very little difference to him. That is why I state that he is responsible for the communist ideas which have taken root in this country; he only protects the wealthy and the trusts to the detriment of the poor people. The country only awaits an opportunity to tell him what it thinks of his high protection and his policy which is contrary to the interests of the people. The last by-elections have proved it and the general election will but confirm my statement.
On April 26, 1934, we had the pleasure of listening to an eloquent speech by the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Gagnon) in support of bill No. 51, which was being discussed by the house. As representative of a
The Budget-Mr. Roberge

Quebec constituency, I was amazed at his attitude towards the hon. Prime Minister of Quebec in connection with a statement made by the latter and published by the newspapers, some time ago. The statement referred to bill No. 51, an act to improve the methods and practices of marketing of national products in Canada. I think that the hon. member for Dorchester should have rather approved the statement of Mr. Taschereau, because he has no right to ignore that the people of the province of Quebec are a minority in this Dominion and must take the necessary steps to see that our rights and privileges granted by the Fathers of Confederation are respected.
I further contend that it was the duty of the Quebec Premier to protest against this new measure which threatens the rights of provinces. The hon. member for Dorchester endeavoured to convince the house that Mr. Taschereau was inconsistent by making this statement, published by the press of the province, and in which he openly opposed this new measure. He had a bill enacted by the legislative assembly so as to permit his government to cooperate with the Dominion government so as to enforce the act, if thought beneficial. I think the hon. member for Dorchester, before criticizing Mr. Taschereau for being inconsistent, should have read the statement the Quebec Premier made when introducing bill No. 243, which permits the provincial government to cooperate with Ottawa, not only as regards Bill No. 51, but with any measure which might be enacted by this house at this session or by order in council, subject to being ratified by the Quebec legislature, at their next session. The hon. Mr. Taschereau stated on that occasion that bill No. 51 had just been introduced in the House of Commons, but that he was unable to say whether the bill would be adopted in its present form or amended so as to protect the rights of our province. The object which the Quebec government had in view when introducing bill No. 243, was simply to be in a position to take advantage of whatever might improve the situation in Quebec, and reject anything which might be detrimental to the interests, as a whole of the province, and it was his right and duty to take such steps.
To follow up what I stated in connection *with Bill No. 51, why did the government, if this bill favours so much the interests of the farmers, delay the measure so long, why did it wait until the eve of an election to introduce it? Had the government adopted
^Mr. Roberge.]
the following resolution moved by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), on October 6, 1932, it might have helped the farming class.
Session 1932-1933, vol. II, page 1544.
Whereas parliament has been in session since October 6, of the present year and is shortly to adjourn until January 30, 1933;
And whereas, since parliament assembled the government has not made any statement of policy with respect to the relief of existing agricultural conditions;
And' whereas, the position of agriculture in Canada has become increasingly deplorable and, unless relieved, will bring about a condition of distress hitherto unparalleled.
This house is of opinion that the government should immediately announce what policy if any, it has with respect to the relief of agricultural distress, and permit full consideration of the same before parliament adjourns over the months of December and January.
By adopting this resolution of the leader of the opposition, the government would have assisted the farming class. It did not then appeal to them, but on the eve of an election they begin to take some interest in the farming class.
The following is the amendment moved by the right hon. leader of the opposition on April 19, 1934:
That all the words after the first word "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
This house, while prepared to support legislation for assisting the orderly marketing of natural products, is unalterably opposed to the enactment of any compulsory measure which delegates to unnamed and undetermined individuals, groups or organizations, sweeping powers over the production and trade and commerce of the nation, and which confers upon a minister of the crown and upon the governor in council unprecedented authority and unusual powers to restrict production, and interprovincial, inter-imperial and foreign trade as regards both exports and imports, as well as other autocratic powers.
According to the official figures which I desire to place on Hansard, the public will have an opportunity of judging for themselves in what way the government takes an interest in the farming class which, in a crisis, should have been helped by >the government.
In the estimates which are voted, each year, on March 31, $7,247,500 were appropriated to agriculture in 1929; in 1930, $8,483,326; in 1931, $8,751,795.24; in 1932, $9,929,908.08; in 1933, $6,671,100; in 1934, $7,365,912; in 1935, $6,510,620. We note a steady decrease, sir, in the appropriations for agriculture, since 1932. Between 1932 and 1935 ,there has been a reduction of more than $3,000,000, while in the appropriations for the Royal Mounted Police-I do not know whether the govern-

The Budget-Mr. MacNicol
ment fears that the country may be kidnapped-there is a steady increase. In 1929, this service received $2,465,375.38; in 1930, $3,040,725.25; in 1931, $3,126,565; in 1932 $3,176,341.34; in 1933, $3,839,595.75; in 1934, $5,615,595.75; in 1935, $5,615,595.75. In looking over the official figures, sir, one may note the little interest which this government displays towards the farming class, since it increases the appropriations for the national defence and reduces those for agriculture, in a time of crisis.
May I, sir, place on Hansard a few of the promises which the right hon. Prime Minister made in 1930, so as to show his great sympathy for the farming class, in the course of the election campaign. How did he keep them?
The following is from the Calgary Herald on June 13, 1930:
We pledge ourselves to foster and develop agriculture and live stock and dairy industries now so sadly neglected.
The Morning Citizen of June 30, 1930, published a speech delivered at Ormstown by the present Prime Minister:
We of the Conservative party maintain that the dominion having control of all systems of taxation must assist agriculture, understand, by scientific study the problems under which we work and get the best returns. And we Conservatives are pledged to see that agriculture receives the same benefits as in the days gone by.
What resulted from these promises? We could quote many others, but these are sufficient to prove to the farming class in what way the right hon. Prime Minister intends to help them, namely, by reducing since 1932, the appropriations for agriculture by $3,419,288.08 and increasing those of the Royal Mounted Police by $2,439,254.41 for 1934-35.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In every budget debate that I have listened to since I became a member of this house hon. gentlemen opposite have apparently enjoyed themselves from time to time in charging that the fiscal policy of the Conservative party is one of tariff barriers, restricted trade, trade obstruction, subserviency to big interests, robber tariffs, exploitation, and so forth. The hon. member for Shelbume-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) added one further expression when he stigmatized the fiscal policy of this government as one of tariff embargoes. At the same time he questioned the efficiency of tariff 74726-189
bargaining as a means to increase the trade of this or any other country. For my part I am in favour of adequate tariffs, and I oppose the stigmatizing of the fiscal policy of this government as a policy of barriers, restrictions, obstructions, embargoes and so forth.
The hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Mc-Phee), when he spoke on the budget, asked: Where is the relief in connection with binder twine? I presume he must have had some thought that the question of binder twine had something to do with the budget now before the house. Ever since the government of the late Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier made binder twine free on January 1, 1898, binder twine has come into Canada free; this government has made no change in that regard, and as far as I know there is no intention whatever of changing the tariff as to binder twine. So why the question was asked I do not know. On the other hand I do know that on the thousand and one items imported into this country, all that are imported from outside the British empire pay an excise tax of three per cent, and those imported from within the British empire pay an excise tax of one and a half per cent. Knowing that the binder twine manufacturers of Canada pay a three per cent excise tax on all the fibre they import to manufacture into binder twine, and knowing that the British manufacturer, who is their second greatest competitor in that commodity, pays only one and a half per cent to ship his finished product into Canada, perhaps the hon. member for Yorkton thought that the Canadian manufacturer was not getting a square deal and had in his mind the idea of giving him some relief.
Since the question of binder twine has been mentioned, I recall having read that when the tariff was taken off binder twine on January 1, 1898, there were some twenty-five plants in Canada making binder twine. To-day there are three. At the time the tariff was taken off binder twine that article sold in Canada at six cents per pound. From the date of the removal of the tariff-I do not mean that free trade was the only cause that brought about this condition-the price of binder twine advanced until in 1918 it was thirty cents a pound. So I say free trade is not a cure-all so far as prices are concerned, but it certainly did put out of commission a goodly number of binder twine companies.
I have spent many years in industry and in association with employment. The principal reason that I am in the house to-day is in



The Budget-Mr. MacNicol
order to do what I can for both employment and industry, because I know they go hand in hand. I know that the tariff does provide jobs.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Gray) may laugh at that, but he has a number of new industries in his own riding as a result of the tariff, and I do not believe the employees in those industries would care to hear him laugh about their employment. I say the tariff has produced and does produce jobs. I am quite well aware that there is exploitation-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -but not necessarily as a result of the tariff. I will give a few instances of exploitation that had nothing whatever to do with any fiscal policy. I have on my desk before me a magazine that records a number of instances of exploitation. I am opposed to price exploitation; I will support any government measure that will prevent it and will see to the punishment of those proven to be exploiters and profiteers. This article, it would appear, refers to instances in the United States. I do not know whether we have had similar instances in Canada, though I do not believe so; I do not think Canadians would do that sort of thing, and I do not cast any reflections on our neighbours to the south. But when a company advertises that a container holds a quart when it really holds only a pint and a half, that is wrong; when containers which are said to contain a pound weigh only fifteen ounces, that is wrong. We all know of the case of the five dollar razor that was protected by patents. When the patents expired German razors were sold in the United States, duplicates of the five dollar razors, for twenty-five cents. Something may be wrong with the patent laws not only across the line but in Canada as well, if such conditions exist; but at any rate I call that exploitation. Then we have the case of a person going to buy an automobile. He is offered 1400 for his old car if he purchases one make of automobile or $800 if he wishes to purchase a higher priced car. I think something is wrong there, because the old car could not in these circumstances increase in value by $400. But the tariff has nothing to do with exploitation of that kind.
