speechtext:
If there is exploitation, however, the government can regulate it or
CMr. MacNicol.]
prevent it by passing laws, and such laws are not new. In the reign of Edward IH the great fishmongers of Billingsgate market threatened to exploit the small fishmongers, and the government of that day, some six hundred years ago, enacted legislation which prevented the great fishmongers from making more than one penny on a shilling's worth of fish. Again, in the reign of Queen Anne, similar laws were enacted to protect the consumers against exploitation. In 1930 the consumers' council bill was introduced in the British house, the fifth clause of which provided that where it was reported to the board of trade that an excessive price was being or was likely to be charged for any commodity, the board of trade might take action. Later that bill was incorporated in the British agriculture bill, and I believe some of the clauses of our marketing act are patterned after the clauses of the British agriculture bill.
The point I make, Mr. Speaker, is that exploitation can and should be prevented by law, but that the true principle of the tariff is not to blame for many cases of exploitation that have occurred. Every hon. member knows that to-day most every nation in the world, great or small, has a tariff. Even the dependencies of the nations have tariffs. Some of these tariffs may be higher and some may be lower than the Canadian tariff; it is not necessary to go into detail. In the face of that situation, however, what is Canada to do? Should she let down her tariff walls, as hon. gentlemen opposite did in 1922, 1923 and 1924? I was in business during those years and I remember the delegations from boards of trade, chambers of commerce and manufacturers from all over Canada that came to Ottawa to protest against the freer trade policy of the late government. I remember it was reported that forty-six per cent of the total capacity of the woollen mills of Canada closed their doors up to 1924, and I know that on September 4 of that year a great delegation attended what was then called an employment conference but what would be called to-day an unemployment conference, held in this city. Facts and figures were submitted to the conference, showing that 1,351 industries of one kind and another, large and small, had closed their doors as a result of the freer trade policy of the late government. Every hon. member knows that up to 1923 and 1924 approximately 350,000 Canadians were thrown out of work in Canada and compelled to migrate to the great republic to the south.

The Budget-Mr. MacNicol
Hon. members opposite also know very well that we could not maintain the Canadian standard of living against competition brought about by freer trade, that the standard of living in Canada would have to go down to the standard of living of lower wage countries. In this connection I should like to read from the speech made by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) on April 29, 1931, as it appears on page 1115 of Hansard for that year. The right hon. gentleman was making an address in connection with unemployment insurance, and just here I may say that I am in favour of a system of contributory, compulsory unemployment insurance. I should like to read this statement, because it is a good exposition of the views held by the right hon. gentleman in that connection. He said:
But there is a law which applies in industrial relations as it does in other fields, whereby if competing standards differ, the lower standard in the course of time, tends to drive out the higher. That law was first enunciated by Gresham with respect to the precious metals.
Gresham pointed out that where two metals were in circulation, the one base and the other pure, the baser metal tended to drive the purer metal out of circulation. That same law, I believe, is applicable ,to competing standards in industry. Where you have high standards of industry in one province, with lower standards in another province, the lower standards, if permitted to compete with the higher standards, will drive the higher standard's out of existence and in time bring industrial standards to the level of the lower.
For that reason it becomes necessary in a country such as ours to devise some means whereby the standards of industry as between the different provinces may be brought to and kept at the same level. I doubt if that is possible in any other way than by some system of federal cooperation or control. But the problem is more far reaching than that. What I have said with regard to industries in the different provinces is equally true of industry as between different countries.
I ask hon. members opposite how they would maintain the standard of living in Canada against the standard of living of, we will say, Russia, Japan, or some other competing nation, other than by an adequate tariff policy. In my opinion there is no other way to do it than by the adoption of a tariff policy. This government has given Canada an adequate tariff policy. If hon. members think it worth while, I would ask them to compare the remarks I am making with the last sentence of the remarks of the right hon. leader of the opposition which I have just quoted. Then I would ask them to review the latest figures indicating the wages paid in some of the leading nations of the world. These figures, based on the eight hour 74726-189*
day and given in the equivalent of Canadian money, show that in Japan they are paying 76 cents per day; that in Italy they have reduced the wages only recently from 95 cents to 85J cents per day. In the Netherlands, where large quantities of binder twine are made and offered as the chief competition for our binder twine, they pay $1.18 a day. Last year the Netherlands sold to this country several hundred thousand dollars worth of binder twine. In France the rate is $136 per day; in Prussia or Germany $1.46; in England $2.28-all these against the average in Canada of $3.42. How can we compete? How can Canadian labour compete-and it is on behalf of Canadian labour that I raise my voice, and which I will defend on every opportunity which presents itself. How can the Canadian worker drawing wages averaging $3.42 compete with the twine worker in the Netherlands drawing $1.18? Apart altogether from binder twine, can the Canadian worker compete in any other way without protection-and I am not by any means in accord with placing a duty on binder twine. On the other hand I am in sympathy with giving the agriculturist every possible opportunity to produce his product at the cheapest possible price, and to sell it in the dearest market he can find. Statistics show that Russian wages to-day approximate 25 cents per day. The Canadian worker cannot compete against that kind of competition, and I know of no other means by which he may be allowed to operate unless through the use of tariffs.
As the time at my disposal is passing rapidly I shall not take time to submit datst and figures to show that business in Canada is getting better. That fact has been admitted from every corner of the house. During the recess I visited twenty-five or thirty towns and cities in Ontario, in addition to travelling extensively in the United States, looking into industrial and labour problems. I visited some sixty to seventy Canadian factories in Canada, talked to managers, foremen and workmen. I know from personal observation that business in Canada is improving. I was glad to find that out. I am pleased to know that every day more and more men are being employed in industry, and I only hope that the improvement continues.
Among other branches of industry I visited were those associated with construction. I must admit frankly that factories engaged in the manufacture of metals, glass, hardware and the allied lines of the construction industry have not improved as rapidly as have many other industries. But they are coming around, which means that construction in Canada is increasing. A person could have

The Budget-Mr. MacNicol
a fair understanding of the amount of construction going on in Canada in comparison with what is in progress in the great republic to the south if he were to visit Philadelphia, which has a population of about 3,000,000. If he were to visit the suburbs of that great city, as I have done, and look into the amount of building going on over there and then return to the great city, one riding of which I have the honour to represent, he would see, as I have seen, that in the suburbs of Toronto there is more construction going on than there appears to be in Philadelphia, a city five times as large. It would do anyone good to visit the northerly limits of the city of Toronto, where there is really a considerable amount of building in progress.
If the government are going to adopt a building program I would say that the sooner they commence the better. I certainly am not in accord with the erection of buildings having no commercial value and which do not effect a saving to the government. With this point in mind, during the recess I visited many Canadian towns and cities and made exhaustive inquiries into matters affecting building construction. For example may I instance the city of Hamilton? I say that Hamilton is entitled to a federal building because at the present time the government has to rent considerable space. In my view a federal building in Hamilton could be erected economically, because it would yield a return in rent saved. All hon. members who have visited Toronto know that on Front street a customs house has been built, but not completed. If the government were to finish the customs house in Toronto the rent saved would in time pay for the work. That kind of construction work is eminently sound, and I am in accord with it. So I would say to the government that at the earliest possible moment they should back up the efforts of the private constructors. So far as I can ascertain there is at the present time building contemplated to the value of $100,000,000. A building program to that extent would mean the employment of 125,000 men working in the quarries, the lumber woods, in the other primary industries connected with building, and would furnish work to the finishers, the artisans who are very anxious to have employment. I endorse heartily the proposal of the government to speed up construction of buildings and particularly those which in due time would pay for themselves.
As I said a moment ago I visited about sixty to seventy factories during the recess. I made a survey of the men engaged in those industries, men who in many instances were

turning out new materials which had never before been manufactured in Canada, materials demanded by Canadians. Capital was invested in those industries because the tariffs of Canada had kept competing materials out of the country. My compilation showed that 10,000 men and women workers are to-day engaged in making brand new material which has never before been manufactured in this country. These workers are in addition to the 400,000 or 500,000 men and women engaged either full or part time in Canadian factories. Some people will say that 10,000 workers do not indicate a great deal of industry, but if one takes the census returns of 1931 he will find that Brockville, Kingston, Belleville, Peterborough, Woodstock, Paris, St. Thomas and Owen Sound combined have only 10,000 industrial workers in their factories, and I will say that any community or province in Canada would be more than pleased to have in their midst a new city with 10,000 workers and with a purchasing power equivalent to that of all the industrial workers in the cities I have just mentioned. And that means more consumers for our agricultural producers in the province of Ontario.
Following the war most countries sought means whereby they could increase their industrial activities. Most of them followed-the plan adopted 'by Germany in 1881. At that time Germany established an industrial council and other European nations followed suit. To-day twenty-two nations have departments of industry, either separate or associated with other departments of government. I would have moved a motion recommending that this government consider the question of organizing a department of industry in this country but I was afraid that industry itself would think there might be government interference. Up to the present I have refrained from recommend|ing anything of that nature, but I am convinced that the time has come when the government could the greater assist the industry of this country without busybody interference. What were the objectives of the German industrial advisory board, the department of industry of France and the departments of industry of Norway, Belgium, Italy, Czechoslovakia, Ireland and China? First, they were organized to provide more jobs; second, to make all jobs more permanent; third, to provide a safer investment for capital; fourth, to provide minimum wage laws for those engaged in industry and compensatory measures where injuries occurred; fifth, to introduce compulsory and contributory unemployment insurance and, lastly, to create a national buying spirit.

The Budget-Mr. MacNicol
Last summer I made a tour of the mines in northern Ontario. I associated with the managers and foremen of mines. One of the things which struck me was the large number of steel drills piled up in the yards of various mines. Upon inquiry I ascertained that up to the advent of this government the mines of northern Ontario imported from New York state seventy-five carloads of steel drills per year. The manager of one of the large mines was impressed with the buy in Canada spirit-in my humble opinion it is patriotic to prefer goods made by Canadians-and he conceived the idea of holding a meeting of mine managers. It was ascertained that not only did the mines of northern Ontario use seventy-five carloads of steel drills but the rest of the mines in Canada used an additional seventy-five carloads, a total of one hundred and fifty carloads per year. I was told that representatives of the steel industry were invited to confer and the result was that to-day a steel plant in an Ontario city is shipping throughout Canada each year one hundred and fifty carloads of steel drills. This industry gives employment to 150 men. That is a real patriotic spirit. If architects, builders * and buyers throughout Canada were imbued with the patriotic spirit to buy Canada made goods, I am satisfied that within a reasonable number of years a quarter of a million more men would be placed at work in this country.
Prior to the imperial conference a deputation of British industrialists came to Canada to confer with Canadian manufacturers. They bargained on what could be manufactured economically in Canada and what British industry could ship to this country. They bargained together, which is not a new thing. Some time ago I read a speech of the Right Honourable Benjamin Disraeli quoted in the Edinburgh Blackwood's Magazine of 1868, at page 369. It appears that in 1844 and 1845 the then Tory Prime Minister of Great Britain was inaugurating a policy of free trade between Great Britain and other countries. His Tory followers were surprised and the common statement at that time was, whither will he lead us. Lord Beaconsfield, then Mr. Benjamin Disraeli, made a speech in which he said in effect:
Not that they were opposed to free trade, so long as it should rest upon sound principle. What they did object to was that, without any attempt to arrange with foreign countries a system of reciprocal intercourse, duties on imports and exports were lessened or repealed which had hitherto supplied the state with an adequate revenue, while at the same time they protected native industry. The party argued thus:	Make, by commercial treaties, any
arrangements which you consider to be advantageous to the common weal. We will
go with you in opening British ports to French silks and French wines, provided France will act in the same liberal spirit towards British cotton goods. We will admit into the home market, at reduced rates, the corn, hemp and tallow of the northern powers, provided they will reduce, in equal proportion, the duties which they now levy on our cutlery and hardware; but don't let us throw away what we possess without getting anything back in exchange, which we shall certainly do if we allow all the nations of the earth to glut our market with their products while they shut our products out of their market by taxing them heavily.
We had an experience similar to that in 1922 and 1923 under the administration of the late government. Our markets were opened to the manufacturers of the world, through low tariffs, while markets of the world were closed to ours. After twenty-five years spent in industry I am satisfied that the state of industry in Canada when the depression came upon us was due to our trade being depressed by the products of labour in foreign countries. The industry of Canada was unable to meet the depression as it otherwise would have done. This government has been eminently wise in taking the course it has in connection with its tariff policy and ensuring the buying by Canadians of goods manufactured in, Canada by Canadian workmen.
I should like to say a word about government costs, because the Minister of Finance pointed out that these costs were being cut down. In my humble opinion industry is afflicted to an abnormal extent with one kind of tax or another. This government has made a splendid start in cutting down the cost of government, but we can go much further when we consider that we have in this country nine legislatures, a legislative council, a House of Commons and a Senate ; approximately one thousand legislators and seventy-five ministers. There is no doubt that the people of Canada are overgoverned, and that the cost of government can be cut down. From 1904 to 1931 the costs of government in this country increased 666 per cent while the population increased only 78 per cent. I congratulate the government on what it has done, but I hope it will go further. Every hon. member has heard of the government costs of the state of South Dakota. In 1932 a new governor was elected and I have before me his inaugural address. I am happy to be able to say that he accomplished much of what he set out to do. He set out to wipe out state banking, state insurance, state bonding, the state railway commission, state operation of mines, state ownership of farms taken over on foreclosures, state duplication

The Budget-Mr. MacNicol
of municipal duties, state duplication of federal duties and state operation of cement and other plants. Governor Tom Berry deserves the support of his state for the attempt he has made to cut down government costs. As one who has been associated with industry for many years, I say emphatically that industry in Canada is crying aloud to this government and every government in the country to cut down the costs which to-day are being inflicted upon it, thus retarding employment to a certain extent. We can do something more along that line.
Many hon. members have no doubt read of the great metallurgical and chemical plant which the Russians are erecting at Magnetogorsk, on the Ural river, occupying about twenty square miles and with a capacity, when it is finally in operation, of four million tons of steel a year. Picture what will happen to the steel trade of the world when that plant goes into full operation. Why, in our palmiest days Canada imported only 150 thousand tons of steel a year. Canada as well as other countries must plan and make every effort to protect themselves against having their markets flooded by goods produced by cheaper labour in other countries. I have no criticism to offer with respect to the wages paid in Russia and the standard of living that prevails there. That is the business of the Russian people, and if they are satisfied with their conditions nothing that we could do, in any event, would alter that. And the same applies to Japan; I do not criticize what they do. Their standard of living and their wages suit them. But I do say that we can protect ourselves against the products of their factories, and we can do so in no way that I know of other than by an adequate tariff. We cannot afford to leave Canadian workmen and factories unprotected against the products of other countries where there is cheap labour. We must have an adequate tariff.
I made an extensive inquiry into labour conditions and industry in Europe and Great Britain, and while there I looked into plant areas and studied the question of plant concentration. I found great industrial areas in Sheffield and Birmingham, but the greatest industrial area in the world in my opinion is Trafford park in Manchester. I made an investigation of plant areas at Halifax, Saint John, Quebec City, Three Rivers and Montreal. All of them have magnificent areas; and along the St. Lawrence river, when the St. Lawrence waterway is completed, we shall have one of the greatest waterways in the world, developing illimitable power. There we shall have one hundred miles of plant sites equal to the

best plant areas anywhere. We have great areas at Vancouver. We have great areas at Winnipeg, at Port Arthur, at Fort William, at Windsor and along the Welland canal. I was happy to learn, while making an investigation of the steel industry in the United States last summer, after this house had risen, the opinion held by one important manufacturer there. He said to me, "Mr. MacNicol, had it not been for the depression this company might have erected along the Welland canal a great steel plant." We have also that magnificent plant area in Toronto which is being exceedingly well developed by the Toronto Industrial Commission. Even during these times of depression, since 1929, under the efficient management of Mr. Keenleyside the Toronto Industrial Commission has brought into that area 115 plants large and small, giving employment to 2,500 men, with an investment of $5,000,000, and occupying 1,250,000 feet of floor space.
I am convinced that if the governments of Canada, federal and provincial, having control over industrial expansion, could organize a department which would work as efficiently- and I see no reason why they should not- as the two great railway industrial departments and other industrial departments have, it would have a very beneficial effect on bringing industry to this country, and such new industry in Canada would provide a good deal of employment for Canadians.
I congratulate the government on what they have done, considering the world depression through which we have been passing, and I say this not only as a former industrialist but for labour as well; for I take second place to no man in this country in my feeling for labour. I say to the government: You have done wonderfully well and you deserve credit, for the employment which you have provided for Canadians, many thousands of men in various industries in this country, as a result of making it possible for much new manufacturing to take place in Canada. I say to them, "Keep on going straight down the road you have been travelling. Be not deterred from your objective, let the chips fall where they may, and in spite of any criticism that may be hurled at you either in this house or outside." I have not the slightest fear regarding the attitude of the people of Canada. They recognize in this government, in the leader and his cabinet, a group of earnest men who have done their best for this country in the severest depression that has ever been experienced not only in Canada but in the world. They have toiled for this country at

The Budget

Mr. MacLean
the sacrifice of their health and I am satisfied that when the bell rings for the general election the people of Canada will rise up and return the Prime Minister at the head of his government to continue as he has been doing.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We are always delighted to hear our good friend from Toronto (Mr. MacNicol) he is always interesting and lucid in his exposition of the tariff policy of this government. But tonight I must congratulate him on his great faith, a faith which is beyond my comprehension, when he suggests that the policy which this government has followed for the past four years will carry hon. gentlemen opposite into the treasury benches after the next election. Time will show how accurate my hon. friend is in that prophecy. I can well understand why he always makes such a plea for the manufacturer and the worker. He comes from an industrial city; his constituency is made up of industrial workers, and it is not to be wondered at that he does his best to put up a plea for them. I am sorry however that the hon. gentleman can see only one side of the question. We on this side of the house see the industrial side, but there is another great class in Canada who must receive some consideration, and that is the consumers and the public at large.
My hon. friend, when I came in, was telling this house that what Canada needed was an adequate tariff. It seems to me that what this government has given the country is a little more than an adequate tariff, for we have the highest tariff that we have ever had. He has also told us what the government has done for industry. Well, the best years that industry in Canada has ever experienced was during the regime of the last government, from 1921 to 1930, when the manufacturers sold more manufactured goods, when our export trade in manufactures was much larger, than at any time in the history of the dominion. And it was not a high tariff that did it but a moderate tariff which provided the country with a revenue so that we were able to pay our way and have a surplus on the right side of the ledger.
I regret the absence of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) from the house tonight and also the very sad reason therefor. The annual budget is always looked forward to with a great deal of interest. It is supposed to give not only a review of the financial situation of the past year but a glimpse into the future, an outline of the policies which the government intends to
follow and also some lead as to our export and import trade. But in this budget speech and in the speeches of hon. members opposite who have spoken in large numbers we have heard nothing regarding our export trade and how they intend to extend it. In the budget there is not one word which suggests that any effort has been made in the past year to secure any new treaties with foreign countries or even to try to put through a reciprocal trade agreement with our friends to the south. Recently we saw that our United States friends were quite willing to introduce legislation looking toward reciprocal trade, and I believe the present is the most opportune time in the history of Canada to make a move in that direction.
We might look for a few moments at the records of the two governments. My hon. friend who has just sat down (Mr. MacNicol) has been a stout defender of his party, and I want to be just as stout a defender of the policies in which Liberal members on this side believe. All we have to do is to review the records of the two parties. No one will deny that under the King administration we had seven years of progress, splendid surpluses and increased trade, but under the regime of our hon. friends opposite, notwithstanding all their promises in 1930, we have had four years of almost famine. It has not yet reached the seven year period, but if our hon. friends remain in office I am afraid that it will run that long. Did the Conservative party give the former Liberal government any credit for the splendid showing they made during their term of office? Not on your life. I remember when sitting on the other side of the house hearing hon. members, then on this side, day in and day out, condemn the former government from every angle-we were spending too much money; we were not showing sufficient surpluses; we were not reducing the public debt fast enough; we were not reducing interest charges sufficiently. Talk about prejudicing the minds of the people! If any persons worked harder than did our hon. friends opposite to prejudice the minds of the people during the Liberal term of office, I would be glad to know it. The present Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) used to tell the house how he would handle the finances of the country. He would provide a sinking fund that would eventually wipe out the national debt; he would reduce interest charges. The right hon. gentleman has had his opportunity; he was elected prime minister in 1930; he was not only prime minister but, for two years of that period, minister a*

The Budget-Mr. MacLean
finance, and he had every opportunity to put into operation the great ideas he had when he was on this side of the house.
But what do we find? The right hon. gentleman, far from moving along the lines he suggested in the house, has never made any effort at all to take care of the financial situation; no sinking fund has been established; deficits have been shown every year. Under the Liberal regime we had seven surpluses amounting in all to 8276,000,000, while our hon. friends opposite in four years have added to the funded public debt no less than
8594,000,000.
Someone may ask: What about the railway debt? Well, what about it? In the seven year period of the Liberal regime the national railways had a deficit of $93,000,000, and even if you take that from the $276,000,000, you have still $183,000,000 of a surplus to go towards reducing the public debt. But even if you disregard that altogether you will find that the public debt has been reduced by a much larger amount than that. When the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) was speaking the other day he pointed out that during the Liberal regime current deficits on the national railways were paid out of current revenues and not charged to the public debt. Our hon. friends opposite should take note of this because it is a fact worthy of a great deal of consideration. Under the Conservative government from 1919 to 1921, the average deficit on the Canadian National was $22,000,000 per annum. From 1922 to 1930 the average surplus for interest payment due to the public was $24,000,000 per annum. The deficits began again when our hon. friends opposite came into power. As I pointed out, one has only to look at page 3 of the public accounts to find that the debt increase from 1930 to 1934 totalled, as I said before, $594,000,000, while increases in interest charges on the public debt, including this year's deficit, have reached $25,000,000. If you include the deficit this year of 8135,200,000. you find that the total interest charge we have to pay in this country is around $145,000,000. When one considers that in 1875 the total debt of the dominion was only $150,000,000, one can see in a minute whither we are drifting.
Coming to the question of interest charges we find that in 1930 the interest charge was around $121,000,000, but in 1933 it had increased to over $139,000,000, an increase of more than $18,000,000 in those three years, while under the Liberal regime interest charges were reduced $4,694,000. As I said before, if we include this year's deficit of $135,200,000 we have now an interest charge of around $145,000,000 per annum.
rMr. MacLean.]
I noticed that some newspapers commenting on the speech of the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth stated that the average deficit of the Canadian National Railways for the last eleven years was $25,000,000. Why do they take the eleven year period? I think it is only fair for each government to stand on its own feet and each one to account for its own deficits or surpluses. If you take the eleven year period you will find from page 19 of the annual report of the Canadian National Railways that the average Canadian National deficit from 1923 to 1929, after deducting the one surplus, was $9,500,000 annually. But the average deficit for the past four years under this government was not $9,500,000 but $58,000,000 annually. That shows the difference in the management under the two parties. Our hon. friends opposite will say: "Oh, that was due to the depression." I think if we want to go into the matter we shall find that the great cause of the falling off of the earning powers of the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific was the fact that this government put on a high tariff that stopped imports. The minute they stopped imports, the transportation systems had nothing to move, the result being that falling off continued right along the line and not only the transportation systems but everything else suffered in proportion.
The Minister of Finance in presenting the budget said that he would have a surplus next year of $8,000,000. I hardly think that is a fair statement to make to the house, because there are a great many things that have not been taken into account. We are told that a bill will be introduced this year providing for the spending of perhaps $50,000,000 on public works. Will these be chargeable to next year's account? If so, what becomes of the estimated surplus of $8,000,000? But it is not only that; there are a great many other items that have not been taken into account. The marketing bill that is now before the house is going to cost quite a few millions to operate if it is operated in the way our friends think it will be. Then there is the cost of restoring the civil service salaries- another large amount. I venture to say that when these items I have mentioned are taken into account instead of having a surplus of eight millions, the balance will be fifty to seventy-five millions on the other side of the ledger. So I say it is unfair to the public for the minister to say: "We are going to balance our budget and have $8,000,000 on the right side," when they knowingly leave out such large items.

The Budget-Mr. MacLean
The same thing happened when the estimates were brought down this year. Headlines appeared in the press all across the continent: "Seventeen millions saved in the estimates." I venture to say that before this house rises supplementary estimates will be brought down that will more than wipe out this seventeen millions. I say again that it is absolutely unfair to treat the public in this way. Our friends opposite should give them the real facts.
When hon. gentlemen opposite were on this side they were continuously telling the house and the public that we were spending too much, that the government was extravagant; that we were proceeding with extensive public works, building railways, erecting buildings, expanding in every way. I remember a small vote I wanted for my county, and the present Minister of Justice was good enough to move that the vote of $11,000 be reduced to SI. That was their idea of economy at that time-they were going to show us how to economize if they got on the treasury benches. Well, here are their expenditures since they have been in power. There was only one year in the ten that the Liberals were in power in which the expenditure exceeded $400,000,000. It ran along from $370,000,000, to $381,000,000,	$351,000,000,
$355,000,000, $358,000,000, $378,000,000, $388,000,000 and $398,000,000. But look at what happened after our friends got into power. In 1931, according to the budget speech delivered the other day, the expenditure was not $398,000,000 as under the Liberals, but $440,000,000 for the first year that hon. gentlemen opposite were in power. The next near, 1932, it was $448,000,000. In 1933 it was $531,000,000 and in 1934 $459,000,000. There is the difference in the expenditure under the two administrations. I do not know how it is in other parts of Canada, but I can say positively that there have been practically no new public works built in the maritime provinces since this government came into power; and the old works have not been maintained as they should be and some are falling into decay. Still our hon. friends have a record of spending from fifty to seventy-five millions yearly more than we spent, and they have nothing to show for it.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about the millions spent at Saint John, for example?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Our friends talk about the tariff situation. Through the kindness of the Prime Minister we had the pleasure recently of hearing the Postmaster General of Australia speak in the restaurant. He said:
It is insensate nationalism, abnormally high tariffs and disorderly marketing methods which, more than anything else, are responsible for delay in the rehabilitation of all nations.
That is not merely the personal opinion of Hon. Mr. Parkhill. Take the reports of the bank presidents at the annual meetings of the banks, until a few years ago nearly every one of them was a high tariff man. I do not think that back in 1928 or 1929 you could find a bank president w'ho was not a high tariff man; at any rate there were very few of them. To-day you cannot find one who will say that an abnormally high tariff such as we have had under this administration has been beneficial to this country. Our total trade dropped from $2,393,000,000 in 1930 to $886,000,000, a decline of no less than $1,507,000,000 since this government came into power.
Then our friends were going to find us new markets, but they have not made much progress in that direction. We have a committee sitting in this house looking into this question from every angle but the right one. What Canada needs is world trade. As was shown by the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Me-Phee) a few days ago, no less than twenty-nine countries have put up their tariffs against Canada since this government came into power. Our hon. friends say, "Oh, the King government was in power for so many years and they did nothing to prevent other countries from raising their tariffs." I heard an hon. gentleman on the other side make that statement the other day. Well, I will tell you one thing the King government did not do; they did not make pilgrimages around the world endeavouring to get other countries to adopt a high tariff policy. We had free entry to Great Britain for our foodstuffs and for everything, from the beginning. My hon. friend who just spoke (Mr. MacNiool) told us about the industries of Manchester. England. What made Great Britain the greatest manufacturing country in the world? Was it her high tariff policy? Not on your life; it was the free trade policy which she followed. Her ships went out on the seven seas and brought in the raw material which was manufactured by her workmen, and she built up the greatest trade and became the greatest nation in the world through that policy. But the Prime Minister of this country made a pilgrimage to Great Britain and endeavoured to persuade that country to put up a tariff against the rest of the world in order that we might obtain a preference there. If the Prime Minister was the means of getting Great Britain to adopt that policy, did he do this country a service or a disservice? I claim

The Budget-Mr. MacLean
that if he was responsible for it he did this country a disservice, because we find that Great Britain has practically served notice on us now that some changes will be made in those preferences, even with the agreements we hear so much about from mu' friends opposite. We had splendid trade facilities with Great Britain, and I do not think there is any doubt that they would have been continued. We never had a written agreement with the mother country until this government -compelled Great Britain to put down in writing rvhat we could and what we could not ship there, and when those agreements run out I think Canada had better watch out or she will find herself shut out from the British market in respect of some of her products.
One of the measures on which hon. gentlemen opposite are staking their reputation is the marketing bill. I think the fact that to-day there were tabled no less than eighteen or twenty amendments to that bill proves that the opposition offered from this side of the house and throughout the country was well founded, because, as I said the other day, if we get a bill that is half workable it will be because the weaknesses of the present bill have been shown up. When you consider that there are only twenty-one clauses in the whole bill and that eighteen or nineteen of those clauses have to be amended I think you will realize in what shape that bill was when it was brought into the house.
Hon. gentlemen opposite have not much to say about the butter question, but I have a great deal of information here with regard to the leakage of butter brought into the maritime provinces. That butter is said to have been released and to have done a great deal of harm to the dairy industry in that part of the country. This is the last thing in the world you would expect under this government, because we all remember what they were going to do for the dairy farmers, how they were going to put them on easy street when they got into power, by shutting out New Zealand butter. Butter to-day is 19 cents. New Zealand butter has been coming in under this government; it is still coming in, and I am afraid that these complaints of leakages are only too well founded.
Hon. gentlemen opposite promised a great many things; very few of those promises have been fulfilled but they took many steps that were not promised at all. When we take the tariff increases into account we find that the government have brought about the largest tax increases that have been put on by any government. We had the sales tax increased

from one per cent to six per cent; the excise tax increased from one per cent to three per cent, and increases in the income tax, the corporation tax and so on, with new taxes imposed on telegrams, long distance calls, pullman car tickets and sugar, and the gold tax imposed just the other day. That does not take into account the tremendous tariff increases put into force by hon. gentlemen opposite, which I see they now admit constitute a direct tax. No, they did not promise these things, but they brought them about. I think if they had fulfilled some of the promises they made in 1930 and left undone some of the things they have done, this country would be in much better condition to-day. The situation is very well summed up in a small quotation from the New Era of Sydney, Australia, which sajrs;
When someone stops buying, someone stops selling. When someone stops selling, someone stops making. When some one stops making, someone stops working. When someone stops working, someone stops earning. When someone stops earning, someone stops buying.
That is just what this government have done. They -have stopped buying from abroad, and when they stopped that we stopped selling. When we stopped selling our factories stopped making, and when they stopped making their employees stopped earning. Then, when the employees stopped earning, everyone stopped buying. That is the situation in a nutshell, and that has been brought about by the policies of this government. I claim that the policy of protection has stagnated trade, crippled business, increased unemployment, ruined our transportation systems, handicapped agriculture, reduced our revenue and brought our country to the verge of bankruptcy. It has increased taxation to an extent hitherto unknown, and all this in the face of promises to reduce taxation, cure unemployment, build up agriculture, find markets, pay old age pensions one hundred per cent and reduce the national debt. Those are some of the promises made by hon. gentlemen opposite which they have not been able to carry out.
The budget speech would lead one to believe that many tariff reductions have been brought about, but I am sorry that these reductions are so few in number. I notice that there is a reduction in the tax on beer, wine and champagne. So far as our province is concerned that does not interest us, because ours is a prohibition province. We do not use liquor, and even if we did want to use it we would not have the money with which to buy it.

The Budget-Mr. MacLean
One matter to which I should like to refer is the tax on sugar. On February 13, 1934, there was a meeting of bakers and candy manufacturers in the city of Toronto, and some startling information was brought out at that meeting. I believe I should put this on record in order to show the increase in duty on this one commodity. These organizations whose names all appear in this statement, state that at the time the meeting was held they could buy one hundred pounds of refined sugar in Cuba for $1.50. The duty amounted to $1.89; the duty on the bag was 4 cents, and there was a dumping duty of 75 cents, bringing the total up to $4.18. Then there was a three per cent special excise tax, which amounted to twelve cents, and the tax of two cents per pound, which make a total of $6.30, including 30 cents freight. So we find that of the total of $6.30 paid for one hundred pounds of sugar, the government took $4.80 in taxes. I say, Mr. Speaker, that there is something seriously wrong with any system that allows any government, whether it be Conservative, Liberal or Progressive, to take $4.80 in taxes out of a total of $6.30, in connection with an article of food that is used every day by both rich and poor. I think that situation should be brought to the attention of the public. I am glad the government reduced the tax by one cent, but in the circumstances I think the tax should have been entirely wiped out. There are other ways of raising revenue without resorting to the taxation of articles of food which are necessities of life.	*
The other night the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Myers) whose pleasing countenance I see across the chamber, told us that the duty on fertilizer did not affect the farmers of this country, and that in fact no fertilizer was brought in on which a duty was paid. I took the trouble of obtaining from the bureau of statistics figures showing the importations of fertilizer, and I find that in the last three years over 16,000 hundredweight of fertilizer were imported. On that amount a duty of $65,880 was paid. That is a snug little sum. And I believe that is not all, because in a circular I have found that since that time a large amount of fertilizer which was not included in the statement I have mentioned, and on which a rate of ten per cent was paid, was brought in. So when hon. members opposite state that the duty does not increase the cost of the article to the consumer, despite the fact that $65,000 is paid in duty, I think we have good indication that duty is being paid and that thereby the cost of the article is increased.
I notice press dispatches indicate that a permanent highway is to be built through the province of Prince Edward Island. That is a very commendable project, and if the government gives assistance to Prince Edward Island we will welcome it. I understand that if the highway is built it will be built out of the unemployment grant, and undoubtedly (he province will have to pay its fifty per cent.
There is just one other point to which I should like to draw attention, and that is that in the past four years we in the province of Prince Edward Island have been left out of the picture. In Ontario no less than $25,000,000 have been expended on the trans-Canada highway, to say nothing of the expenditures in the other provinces. Large expenditures were made in the last two years in Nova Scotia, and it would seem that Prince Edward Island has been left out of consideration when the moneys were being handed around. Someone will say that it is because we had no unemployment down there. Well, Mr. Speaker, I wish to state that we did have considerable unemployment. There is this to be said about our people, however, that they will put up with a great deal, and that they are mostly able to get three meals a day in some kind of way. We did have unemployment, and could very well have used a considerable amount of the unemployment money in the building of a highway which by this time could have been completed. I believe the press behind the Prime Minister stated during the last election campaign- and I am glad to see him coming into the chamber, because he can correct me if I am wrong-that it was the policy of the Conservative party to establish a national highway system, which would mean that all the roads in Prince Edward Island would be taken over and maintained by the federal government, thereby reducing taxation in the province. Then, prior to the provincial election the late premier, Mr. Stewart, visited Ottawa and upon his return stated to the press that the Prime Minister of Canada would carry out his policy of federal assistance to the highways in Prince Edward Island. All I wish to say is that for the past three years no work has been started. As I have pointed out, the other provinces have benefited to a great extent in the expenditure of relief money, and I am pleased to know that a start is to be made in Prince Edward Island. I hope it will be a good start, and that a good road will be built.
Mr. Walter M. Stewart

In conclusion may I say that we have been asked to depend on the resourcefulness of our people, and have been told that if we do that, undoubtedly we will pull through the depression. Well, in 1930 hon. members opposite did not want even the resourcefulness of the people; they felt that they themselves were sufficient to put policies into effect which to a great extent would improve conditions. I regret that these improvements have not taken place, and that the reverse is true. I believe that the country is ready for a chance to vote, and the people are asking the government to give them that opportunity. When that time arrives I am convinced that the people will record their vote in favour of the party which during the last ten years they were in power gave to Canada an era of prosperity unequalled in its history.
On motion of Mr. Fraser (Cariboo) the debate was adjourned.
On motion of Mr. Bennett the house adjourned at 10.40 p.m.
